speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, September 20, consideration of Bill C-110, to amend the Export Development Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 6 and 8 (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker,
1 am pleased to be able once again to speak on Bill C-l 10. A study of the Export Development Corporation was done by the Economic Council of Canada recently and I wish to add to the record the recommendations which were made. First, they recommended that the Export Development Corporation gradually move toward providing export credit reinsurance leaving the field of insurance proper to the private sector. They further recommended that the Export Development Corporation serve as the insurer of last resort to close any gaps left by the private sector in the supply of export credit insurance.
They also recommend that the Export Development Corporation continue to provide direct financing for Canadian sales abroad when there is reason to believe that the private sector is unable to provide the required credits.
Public financing should be made available only under terms and conditions commensurate with the risks involved and the costs of such assistance, including the opportunity cost of the funds used, except in those cases where it is deemed necessary to take into consideration the export support programs of other countries.
They further recommend that the Export Development Corporation's gradual withdrawal from most direct lending activities be accompanied by an increased concentration of its efforts in the field of credit insurance and bank guarantees.
The corporation should also stand ready to provide refinancing facilities for private lending institutions engaged in export finance.
They recommend that the federal Government continue its efforts at meetings of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development and the General Agreement on Tariffs
and Trade to obtain an international agreement to limit further subsidized export credit. In the absence of such an agreement, they recommend that Canada use subsidized credit only in cases where there is a sufficiently strong presumption that it will facilitate the opening of new markets or that it will increase the market share for Canadian products.
Further, they recommend that in the absence of an international agreement to limit further subsidized export credit, the federal Government consider the advisability of matching foreign export support programs that currently have no equivalent in Canada and of providing assistance to domestic firms which must compete with imports that have benefited from foreign subsidized credits. They recommend that the private sector be encouraged to supply direct export credits to its Canadian producers even when a public subsidy is deemed necessary. The federal Government, through the Export Development Corporation, should assume the cost difference between the preferential conditions offered and the conditions that would have prevailed had private financing been offered in the absence of public support.
[DOT] (DIO)
Also they recommend that the EDC manage separately those of its activities intended to expand markets for Canadian products. They further recommend that provision be made for greater co-ordination between the Export Development Corporation and the Canadian International Development Agency whenever their activities overlap.
1 support Motions Nos. 6 and 8 presented by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) which will nullify the Government's proposed increase from $2.5 billion to $10 billion.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise again to participate in this debate on amendments to the Bill and to point out firmly to the Canadian taxpayer that the principle of this Bill is not trade, that we on this side do not oppose the Export Development Corporation and that the Progressive Conservative Party, in principle, stands four square behind trade. Canada is, and must be, a trading nation. Some 40 per cent of our Gross National Product comes from trade. Our own Member, the Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), was one of the ablest Trade Ministers in Canadian history.
No, Mr. Speaker, this Bill is not an EDC Bill, it is an ANT Bill. EDC stands for Export Development Corporation. ANT stands for accountability, need and trust.
Let us look first at accountability, or rather the lack of accountability that we have seen over the years on the other

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
side of this House. Bill C-110 as proposed by the Grits will increase to $62 billion what the EDC can borrow, lend and insure without the consent of this House, without even the audit of the one watchdog we have who we can trust, the Auditor General. So much for accountability. In reality, none, Mr. Speaker, and that is why we urge Members opposite to support these needed amendments to protect the taxpayers of Canada, on whose behalf we were sent to this august place.
Let us look at need. Motion No. 6 would not allow the Government to increase the limit of promissory notes to $10 billion from the present $3.5 billion, as provided in the Bill. Does the Government need that increase? No. Why not? Because it has expended only 80 per cent of its present limit. In other words, there is no need.
Motion No. 8 would not allow loans through the Consolidated Revenue Fund to be increased from the present limit of $2.5 billion to $10 billion. Again, we find that the Government has not reached the present limit in this regard. It is at some $700 million as against the $2.5 billion limit. Again, there is no need, no demonstrated need.
These amendments now before you from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) are a genuine attempt to regain some measure of control over the activities of a Crown corporation that last year showed an actual profit on capital of $691 million. At first blush that would seem fine, but when you delve into the matter a little bit, you find that is a rate of return of one-tenth of I per cent. Ask somebody in the free enterprise world what that means in the running of a corporation. Does this corporation need even more funding and an even freer rein? I believe not. There is no demonstrated need.
Should that need arise, then the Government should come before this House and show the need is there. It should account for the need and, of course, in that manner the decision would be made right here and the Canadian taxpayer would be protected. Again, the Government should be accountable and show need. Our concern on this side of the House is first accountability, second need, and third trust.
Should we trust this Government with $62 billion in the EDC? This is a Government which has given us a $31.5 billion deficit and a total deficit which costs every man, woman and child in Canada $4,768. That is a 508 per cent increase since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office in 1968. This is a Government which wants to rule by Crown corporations. It has given us the invisible record of the post office. We have the CBC with a $700 million price tag. It is ours, Mr. Speaker. Then we have a measly $2 billion loss in Canadair. It is ours. What about the loss in de Havilland at $500 million? It is ours. This is a Government which has destroyed the petroleum industry with Petro-Canada to the tune now of probably some $8 billion. It is surely ours.
[DOT] (ins)
Is this the trust Canadians should accept? Should we trust the Government, or should we be pointing out to Canadian taxpayers, as I am hopefully doing right now, the need for our
amendments? Hon. Members opposite should realize the need for these amendments, the need for accountability and the need for a new government that Canadians can trust.
In my nomination and many following speeches, I attempted to alert Canadians to the fact that the goal of the present Prime Minister was two fold-a bilingual nation and the redistribution of wealth. This redistribution of wealth is taking place right now through the burden of tax on the productive end of society and through Government control by Orders in Council and Crown corporations. But, even worse, these Crown corporations now have the say and control of the creation of wealth as well as its redistribution through FIRA, CIDC, CIDA, IRDC, EDC, et cetera. Bureaucrats are making the decision as to where wealth shall be directed, not free enterprise. This is still a free enterprise country but the bureaucrats are making these decisions without accountability.
We see this intervention almost daily with Canadair, de Havilland, Eldorado, Canada Post, Massey-Ferguson, Chrysler, Maislin, the fisheries industry-state control of the fisheries industry-and Air Canada. The bureaucratic, socialist eggheads surrounding the Prime Minister are slowly but surely strangling this Canada of ours. They have never met a payroll, let alone an accounts payable, so what is a $31.5 billion deficit to them? It is a method of applying the screws with more and more state control. To the question "Do you trust this Government?" Canadians by the polls have answered no. It is small wonder with the Government's philosophy and record of strangling us by Crown corporation control. What do Canadians ask for? They ask for ANT-accountability, need and trust. They do not ask for EDC. We on this side of the House, unlike ants, will not be crushed underfoot. We demand through our amendments accountability.
What about the board of the EDC? Is there a preponderance of hard-nosed business people on it? Of course not, not with this Government. Bill C-110 will simply be another step on the road to Liberal Government Crown corporation control by overtaxation, with outside representation; a corollary to the cause of the United States War of Independence.
In 1982 the Auditor General expressed the following concern:
Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds... Parliament should give attention to issues surrounding control and accountability of those mixed enterprises and other entities and associates in which the Crown is a shareholder.
The amendments we are discussing today are an attempt to do just that. It is disappointing that the initiative was not taken by the Government, but it is not surprising, given its lack of concern for parliamentary control over the public purse.
On June 10, 1982 I rose in my place to decry runaway Government spending, in particular the IRDC and the CIDA. In his 1979 report, the Auditor General indicated:
A significant factor affecting CIDA's Estimates is that it has been obliged to obtain legal authority for its operations through appropriations acts, because there is no act of Parliament establishing the Agency and delineating its authority.
September 22, 1983

Cl DA costs us $2 billion per year. It is very interesting to see the types of loans which Cl DA makes, and a person from Cl DA will be sitting on the board of EDC and making decisions. 1 wouid like to give a rundown of some of the things Cl DA has done.
It has given special assistance loans to developing countries during the year, and additional loans to Turkey were authorized by votes. It then lists a litany of horrors: a "twenty-year maturity, five-year grace period at 5 per cent interest per annum, maturing September in the year 2000, $18,958,697". In order to prop up the Bank of Canada we borrow at 16 per cent and then give away money with these loans. Under (g) of the same report, it lists a "50-year maturity, ten-year grace, interest-free, maturing at various dates between March 2003 and March 2031 for $1,953,618,922". This is the type of thing that CIDA is doing for us, and there is someone from there being appointed to the Board of EDC.
I see you nodding at me, Mr. Speaker. It is obvious that this Government with its phalanx of Crown corporations has been unable to reverse the downward slide of our economy. Indeed, it has been the major part of the cause. It is time to call on the private sector to get Canada back on its feet again. My hon. friend's amendments are a step in that direction, and 1 support them wholeheartedly.

Mr. Speaker, during the last few years we in Canada have been witnessing the disappearance of parliamentary democracy. This Bill is another step toward destroying what it has taken generations to build. There was a time when taxation and the expending of money was the responsibility of the monarch or the Government, whatever that Government happened to be. That was not satisfactory to the British people. Therefore, in 1215 representatives of the British people met with King John. They told him they wanted no more taxation without representation and no more expenditures without the approval of the people. That was embodied in the Magna Carta, which is the basis of British liberty.
Since that time we have seen the evolution of a system of parliamentary representation that has been the finest in the world. The late Winston Churchill said there may be some things wrong with our type of parliamentary representation, but when we compare it with the alternatives, it stands head and shoulders above all the others.
Under the Prime Ministership of Pierre Trudeau, we have not seen this evolve as we did under the late Mr. Diefenbaker, Mr. St. Laurent or Mr. Pearson. The leaders of the Progressive Conservative Party from Mr. Stanfield to the Right Hon. Joe Clark, to our present leader, Mr. Mulroney-

-and the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney), are concerned because parliamentary representation and parliamentary procedure are not evolving or unfolding as they should. As a matter of fact, we see that the reverse is happening. Instead of seeing the evolution of the parliamentary representation of the people, we are seeing the devolution of it. We are seeing the devolution of parliamentary practice.
This Bill is a typical example of how we are losing control of the public purse. If Parliament loses the control of the public purse, what else has it got? Parliament must control the public purse. If not, we might as well dissolve Parliament. The whole issue rests on whether or not we are to control the amount of taxes that the people will pay and the amount of money that the Government will spend.
Under the British parliamentary system, the Government has no right to spend any money that has not been approved by the Parliament of that country. But we in Canada are seeing the devolution rather than the evolution of Parliament. By the word "devolution", I mean the descent through a series of changes. We are sinking lower and lower, which is what my friend, the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) meant when he said that they are gradually strangling Parliament.
We see the results of this strangling of Parliament when we look at the people of Canada. There are a million people unemployed. People are afraid to invest any more money because we no longer control the public purse. The Government spends as it wishes and taxes as it wishes.
Let us look at this Bill which is only one of many typical examples of this loss of control. Let us look at Clause 7 of the Bill that is now before us. This Clause deals with Section 14 of the Act and does not provide for the ascent of parliamentary control but for the descent of parliamentary control. We are now increasing the amount that can be spent by Order in Council, money over which we have no control, from $3.5 billion to $10 billion. The situation was bad enough under the previous Act when Cabinet could spend up to $3.5 billion by Order in Council to use to go around the world to ensure poor deals and endorse promissory notes. But it is not $3.5 billion any more; now under this Bill it goes up to $10 billion. This is the devolution of parliamentary practice.
The amendment to this Bill will take us back to the point where we can begin to practise parliamentary procedure once again. At least we will be back to the point we were at under the present Act. I do not believe we have the authority to go beyond that. However, 1 would like to see it reach the point where only in the case of very specified items, Cabinet or the executive council may spend money without parliamentary

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
approval. Even that spending should be approved in principle before the people's money may be spent by Order in Council.
That is what Clause 7 of the Bill does when it repeals Section 14 of the Act. This Clause gives Cabinet the authority to spend far beyond the amount it was authorized to spend before. Now by Order in Council, the Cabinet can spend up to $10 billion without referring to the representatives of the people. If King John had used that practice, there would have been a revolution in England rather than simply a body of men meeting him at Runnymede. Those men would have hit him so hard that he would never have recovered. That is what should happen now.
The Government does not have the approval of the people to destroy Parliament, but that is what it is doing. Under this Government, we are witnessing the devolution of Parliament. We are witnessing, step by step, its gradual descent through a series of changes. That is why this particular Bill should be amended so that Cabinet must go back to Parliament to seek approval in principle before it spends any money. That is the difference between Moscow and Ottawa. But the difference is becoming less and less; we are becoming more like Moscow and less like London, England.
In London, England, the Labour Party, the Conservative Party and every other Party that I was able to see, are anxious to preserve the control of the public purse in the hands of the people. That is democracy. We see the reverse in this country and I am getting sick and tired of the Government becoming more and more like Moscow. I did not don the uniform so that we could have a dictatorial, totalitarian Government in this country, and neither did the thousands of young men and women who died in the last two World Wars; they died so that we could preserve democracy and have control of the public purse. The Government is betraying the people with this Bill and with several other Bills.
Let us consider the other clause that we propose to amend. The Leader of the Opposition is determined to correct this state of affairs. When he is Prime Minister of Canada-which will be just as soon as the Government has the nerve to call an election-we will start to evolve parliamentary procedure and stop this devolution. Most Canadians say that the sooner that happens, the better. Let us turn to Clause 8 of the Bill-

I feel equally strongly on the important issue under debate, however, perhaps not about the technicalities of Motions Nos. 6 and 8, but, rather, about the underlying principle. That principle is that by granting the Government the authority it requests, Parliament and the people of Canada will lose control over what is going to happen over the next ten years or so with the Export Development Corporation.
The amendment we propose to Clause 14 would reduce or limit the amount of insurance and guarantee that can be issued by the Export Development Corporation to $3.5 billion. That is still a rather large sum of money but it is nothing like the $10 billion authority that the Government requests. It is nowhere near the present ceiling either, and it is evident that a number of years would pass before the ceiling of $3.5 billion, the one we propose to retain, was reached.
Similarly, Motion No. 8, which deals with Clause 18, would limit the maximum liability of foreign Governments. The amount of money that the Export Development Corporation could loan overseas would be $2.5 billion instead of the $10 billion that the Government proposes. Here again, our reasoning is very similar.
As an illustration of what we on this side of the House have been saying for the last ten days or so that the matter has been debated, I should like to quote from yesterday's issue of The Globe and Mail. An article in the business section begins as follows:
In a follow-up to its decision to reopen a $680-million (U.S.) loan agreement with Romania, the federal Government has authorized the Export Development Corp. to offer up to $535-mi!!ion (Cdn.) in export insurance to Canadian banks and suppliers.
Later in the same article this appears:
The Order-in-Council from the federal Cabinet authorizing the insurance said EDC's board of directors believes contracts will "impose upon the corporation a liability in an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to the country".
Evidently Hon. Members opposite have not listened to what we have been saying for ten days. In the middle of a debate on accountability and the way that decisions respecting the Export Development Corporation should be made, out it comes with an Order in Council reversing the position taken by the board of directors of that Corporation.
In this case the board, which is predominantly people in the employ of the Government, acting prudently, suggests that there is no way we should authorize $535 million insurance in connection with the Romanian deal. The Government does not want to take that advice, however. It has its own ideas and it probably has some friends in the business. It insists, by Order in Council made in secret, that the EDC incur this further half billion dollar indebtedness-or what could become an indebtedness-at a time when the insurance claims upon the EDC in
September 22, 1983

the last 12 months are almost twice as much as they were in the previous 12-month period.
1 strongly suggest that when decisions of this kind are taken, they should be taken in the open. There are good reasons why Parliament and the people's representatives should be able to debate the provision of a half billion dollar insurance in connection with the Romanian deal. The board of directors of the EDC has said that it is not a good business deal. From the strictly business point of view the deal does not make sense and we should not enter into it. The ability of Romania to make good on its financial promises is not certain and in the opinion of the board of directors it does not justify this amount of insurance.
There are other reasons why this matter should be debated publicly instead of the decision being made in secret in the Cabinet room and, 1 suppose it is hoped, without the public knowing anything about it. I am sure that is what was in the minds of Members of the Cabinet when the decision was made. Not only is the question of business prudence applicable but the Romanian deal also involves nuclear power plants and nuclear material. Should we be making deals to supply fissionable nuclear materials to Romania? It is not the most friendly country toward Canada. It has a great deal of association with Warsaw Pact countries. Is it a sensible thing for the taxpayers of Canada to subsidize the export of nuclear materials to an eastern bloc country like Romania?
There is another point that some of my friends in the NDP may want to bring up if they have an opportunity to debate this matter-and they have not had an opportunity-and that is the history of human rights in Romania. People in Canada have often said that perhaps taxpayers' money should not be used to subsidize commercial relations with countries that have a rather poor human rights record. I think there is some validity in that point of view. This issue should have been debated in Parliament by the people's representatives before the decision was made.
in my submission, Mr. Speaker, frontbench Members on the opposite side have not listened to one single word we have been saying about public accountability of Crown corporations. The obsequious Members on the backbenches opposite have just sat quietly. They have not entered into the debate at all.

In any event, this is a very important Bill to our Party because it shows the philosophical difference, perhaps, between what the Progressive Conservative Party would like to do and what the present Government has been doing for the last 15 years and wants to continue to do.
I would like to point out that our Party is not against the Export Development Corporation. In fact, we have probably been the Party in this House which has been its closest friend over the years since the corporation was first formed some 20 or 30 years ago. The fact is that with the present limits which it is allowed under the existing legislation, we do not even have to be here discussing this Bill. The Export Development Corporation could probably go on for another five years before it runs out of the funds which it presently has allotted to it.
The Export Development Corporation presently has the right to guarantee or co-sign loans and insurance for $3.5 billion. That is under the present legislation. In the last ten or 12 years since this legislation came into force, it has used up only $400 million of those funds. Therefore, it still has eight times the amount it has already used before it will have used up its entire amount. Why are we sitting here debating a Bill to increase that ceiling from $3.5 billion to $10 billion if the corporation has only used $400 million of the line of credit it is allowed? And it has taken it ten years to use that.
Clause 18 would allow the federal Cabinet to make direct loans, similar to clause 14. Once the Export Development Corporation and its board of directors have said: "No way we want to insure this loan", that is when the Cabinet, by Order in Council, can move in and say: "Oh, well, we do not care about the board of directors-which we hand-picked. We thought they were very bright. But we, as the Cabinet, have decided to overrule those independent-minded Canadians who are the board of directors and we, as the Cabinet, feel that we will do it anyway." By Order in Council, the Cabinet can overrule the board of directors and the Export Development Corporation and give direct loans rather than guaranteed and insured loans, and it wants again to increase the ceiling from $2.5 billion to $10 billion. The $2.5 billion ceiling has been in existence for ten or 12 years now, and the Export Development Corporation has used up only $700 million. It has used up only one-third in ten years. Why the big rush to increase this ceiling? The fact remains that the Government wants to give control to the Cabinet in order to spend money beyond parliamentary scrutiny.
What has it done to help the people of our country? There is a provision within the Farm Credit Corporation Act wherein the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) qan go to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and ask if the Farm Credit Corporation can borrow some money. This summer the Minis-

ter asked Cabinet if he could borrow just $650 million to lend to Canadian farmers in order to help them over a period during which they have had difficulty. The Minister of Agriculture was turned down by his own colleague, the Minister of Finance, when he asked for that $650 million. He was given $250 million, which has already been used up, and there is another few months to go in this year. The Government will not even allow another institution to borrow money in order to help Canadians; it wants to have control in the hands of Cabinet, outside of the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation, so it can sign the deals or make the loans, on political porkbarrels, from one end of the country to the other, so we can export the goods represented by this money abroad. Too bad for the Canadian farmers, but, "Hello, Algeria, we are going to give you $100 million. Canadian farmers, too bad. Go bankrupt. We are not going to give you any loans". That is unfortunate.
The whole reason we are debating this Bill, as a Party, is that we believe Parliament should have control, and retain control, of the purse strings. The Canadian taxpayers have sent us here. They have said to us: "We are sending you as our representatives to demand accountability for how our money is being spent. We do not want to give this Government a blank cheque. It has been using one for 14 years. Now take hold of the purse strings." Any poll which has been done shows that the Canadian people right now do not trust the present Government. They think that the present Government is throwing money around in a crazy way. They believe it is improper for us to be running deficits of $30 billion. Last year it was $28 billion. The year before it was $18 billion. Government has increased the national debt over six times since it has become the Government.
The Canadian people want to trust their politicians and their Government, but I can tell you right now, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people do not trust their politicians. They are put on the same level as used car salesmen or worse, because the Government does not spend their money wisely. The Canadian people know that even if they do not have to come up with the dollars to pay off the debt today, their children and their children's children are going to have to pay off the debt. There is not going to be a bright future in this country. The people want to have faith in their elected representatives, but they do not have it right now. They want to have trust in their governments, but they do not have it right now. The Canadian public have sent their representatives here to exercise parliamentary control over how their tax dollars are being spent. We do not have that right now. The Government want the right, in the totality of this Bill, to spend $62 billion without ever having to come back to Parliament again. It does not even want to tell us what it is spending the money on; it just wants a blank cheque for $62 billion. That is what this Bill says.
If the Government is not going to be held accountable to the taxpayers as to how it spends their money, then the Government should have the courage to fold up this place, disband
and become a dictatorship or a one-party system. The whole reason Parliament is here is accountability.

Do they have the faintest idea where that money goes? It is terrible for me to report to them that I cannot find out in the House of Commons or its committees. And why not? Because this Government over the years had a deliberate policy and philosophy-and I say deliberate-of ensuring that no one can find out where the money went, where the tax dollar was spent and why it was being spent.
We get the odd horror story, yes, but would it not be much more sensible if first of all Government departments had to put their figures out in an annual report in a meaningful way so that any Member of the Opposition, or of their own Party, could look at those figures and see what was going on? I defy anyone to take an annual report of any Government department, despite whatever accounting training they may have had, and make sense of it. There is deliberate, absolutely deliberate obfuscation of figures, deliberately misleading figures, deliberately attempting to evade responsibility and make the situation incomprehensible not only to the Opposition but to the Government's own Members on the backbenches.
Gentlemen, we were sent here to do a job, but with an arrogant Government and Cabinet, with Deputy Ministers who really think they run the country, and do under the regime in power then the key factor is that until you have a Government in this country which is prepared not only to trust the people but also to trust the Parliamentarians to do their job properly, we will continue to slide down the drain. And we are sliding down the drain. All you have to do, Mr. Speaker, is look at the deficits of this Government. But do you really get an opportunity to see, as an example, what the Department of Communications is spending on this, that and the other thing?
Export Development Act
There is such a thing in business as value for money. Everyone understands value for money, but how do we find out what value we get for our money from a Government which will not tell you anything? That is what this Bill is all about. That is why we are fighting it so hard, because we are being asked to take a figure like $62 billion and not be responsible for it at all. I do not know where this Government thinks the money comes from, but 1 can tell the Government that it comes from the individual taxpayer and he has a right to know, and 1 have a duty to complain bitterly when I cannot get for him those figures.
There is no way I am going to know from this Bill, what happens to the money, Mr. Speaker. I might find out five or ten years from now that the corporation has wasted $10 billion on something, but I am not going to find out in time to do anything about it. I am not going to find out in time to make it responsible to the Canadian people. What I am talking about is the philosophy of a group of power-mad Cabinet Ministers, a group of power-mad Deputy Ministers and senior civil servants whose main job seems to be to make sure that nobody in Parliament knows what goes on. There just is no accountability and that is what this whole thing is all about.
I think the idea of the Export Development Corporation makes sense, but how it has been run, whether it has been effective or whether it has been a political toy with bad loans and bad insurance risks, I as a Member of this Parliament will never be able to find out. That is a tragedy for the Canadian people. It is a tragedy that I have to tell those people who voted for me and sent me here that 1 am sorry but, because of the present regime's philosophy of government which says "we will not tell you, you are never going to find out, forget it, just rubber stamp the legislation," I cannot tell them. That means to me that I am not doing my job; not because I do not want to but because 1 cannot.
The numbers on the other side tell me that 1 cannot because they simply will not make that information available to permit not only the Opposition but their own Members to know what is going on. This is government by clique. This is government by secrecy. This is government by arrogance and disregard for the true meaning of the House of Commons the true meaning of democracy. It shows a colossal contempt for the Canadian public. May the public wake up one day and take a good look at what this gang has done and how it has done it and realize that it is to their detriment to leave it in place.
I close by asking Members opposite to understand how they are destroying democracy, accountability and good sense in this country, because that is what they are doing.

Mr. Speaker, I think the issue has been dealt with very well in the House today. Several Members have expressed themselves differently but all have said the same thing. What we are witnessing is not only true in this House but true in almost every form of legislative arena in the world.

September 22, 1983

I believe what the last Member in particular, who is a new Member, was saying is that he does not really get mad at these fellows across the way; he just really feels sorry for them because they have to take orders from people who are not accountable. If those people want all the money in the world and do not want to report it, those Members have to say that that is what is good for the country. We should not be angry with them when they surrender their freedom to their own employees; we should feel sorry for them that they want to hang on to their positions because it gives them prestige some place. The fact is that all governments in the world have surrendered the power which they have under the constitution, which was achieved by the struggles of our forefathers to control our own destiny, to a self-styled elite.
I speak with some experience and feeling about this issue. This control which is held by small groups that exert control in our bureaucracies must be challenged. It must not only be challenged by the Conservative Party here but by all parties in every country of the world. The situation is just as bad in China, Russia, Belgium, France and Italy. Governments can change every week in France without making any difference; the same people run the country.
Why is this challenge important to Canada? Our future lies in free trade world-wide. If we want to keep peace in the world, the only proven technique to keep and maintain peace is to trade with people. It is necessary to do this so that we do not fall under the umbrella of paranoia where confused pilots fly on dark nights over strange areas. Even the government in Moscow does not know what is going on. The blundering goes on. Everyone is quick to jump on this paranoia issue and become excited and frightened, when the real issue facing Russia, Canada and the United States is how to control this monster that has been created in an effort to have people govern themselves.
I happen to deal with this type of problem quite often. I spent the last three days in New York and Pittsburgh talking about these very issues with several nations. The problem we face is how to get around the set-in-tablet mentality of governments all over the world. For instance, Europe has very restrictive legislation, regulations and techniques for stopping the flow of food into that area. With food they also include things related to health, such as medical equipment and so on. To the cynical person, this is simply a way of putting a high tariff around European nations. Europeans have a reason to be frightened since they have gone through two serious wars in the last 80 years. The people in Russia and other countries are frightened and want to protect their own supply of locally-produced food. Therefore these arbitrary restrictions are applied.
Let us look at the Middle East where new governments come into being. If we look at the legislation of the 21 nations in the Middle East, which covers North Africa and the golden area of the Euphrates, Tigris and so on, every one of these nations has copied the restrictive legislation of European countries. They are terrified that some kind of food will come into their area which will hurt their farmers and their health. They will not let food or anything healthy go into their countries
until they are sure that it has met these restrictive regulations. While these restrictive regulations in Europe are mainly a protective device at the current time since they have highly qualified people and productive agriculture, the Middle East countries, which desperately need food and health care items, follow the same regulations. They are controlled by the dead hands of the government or the bureaucracy that must follow the rules.
These problems are resolved not by dealing with government organizations on one side or the other but by dealing with private groups in each of these countries in determining how to meet all of these regulations without the governments feeling cheated. In this way the goods can get moving.
This is particularly noticeable in the health medical services. For example, the Saudi Arabian government has spent billions of dollars commencing the building of a hospital and medical system. It wishes to expand it by another 7,000 beds. It wants to spend approximately $2.3 billion putting in 7,000 more beds as well as all the services, supplies and maintenance. It has not gone to other governments for help but has asked private enterprise groups in Canada to get together and determine what its needs are, to build a consortium and bid on these contracts.
The Saudi Arabian government is faced with the closed shop organizations of two big enterprises in the United States, France and England which are very good at this type of thing. Since that government feels Canada is not as far down the slope as these other countries, it would like a country such as ours to put in a bid which will force those other nations to be competitive. In other words, it has decided that running its hospital through the government makes it a complete sucker for those people who sell it things. They want to put this project up for tender in order to reduce costs and in hope that it will be operated privately from outside so it can get greater efficiency at less cost and still provide the quality of service.
This is an opportunity for Canadians to participate but we are up against the fact that most Canadians wait for the Government to do it. They want it to go before the Export Development Corporation in order to provide money. That is not how to do it because private enterprise has to keep free from the Government to get a chance to win those contracts in Saudi Arabia.
What I have said in detail illustrates the type of problem that exists in trading. It goes back to putting everything under control of a government organization that does not tell the people what it is doing and allows for all sorts of things to happen.
What I have said about Saudi Arabia I could repeat for trading between Taiwan and Canada or trading between Taiwan and the People's Republic of China and so on. I think I have emphasized the point enough. The answer to the opportunities that exist is not just giving more money to a government agency but to put into the thinking of those around this agency the ideas that will achieve the purpose at

less cost to both sides. You cannot operate behind a curtain; it does not work. Operations of that sort are not trusted by the other fellows and you will not get much forward progress.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to speak to this Bill, particularly following the very statesmanlike speech given by the Hon. Member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton).
Bill C-l 10 is an Act to amend the Export Development Act. There is a series of amendments to this Bill which attempt to restrict the amount of money which will be available to the Export Development Corporation without reference to Parliament.
Much as I can support the aims of the corporation, I must indicate a great deal of sympathy for the concern which has brought these amendments before this House. Right now about 26 per cent of our Gross National Product is directly dependent upon the export market. A fairly hefty portion of that 26 per cent is related directly or indirectly to agriculture. At no time in my understanding has the Export Development Corporation been used to develop the direct growth of agricultural production. In fact, where opportunities have arisen in the last few years, such action has not been taken by the corporation, partly because of the terms of the Act and partly because the Act was not interpreted to assist the sale of agricultural products.
For instance, just in the last year the Government has withheld credits for grain sales to several countries, countries such as Poland. The Government has given very spurious reasons for not giving these credits for the purchase of grain, such as the fact that Poland cannot pay its bills. We can agree that Poland is having difficulty payings its bills, but so are Mexico, Brazil and Chile. In each latter case we have extended credits to those countries. The loss of these kinds of sales to countries like Poland affects the cash flow of the farmers, which consequently affects the welfare of the western agricultural industry.
I have two suggestions regarding this particular situation which I would like the Government to look into. First, I think it is time the Government looked at this Bill, and the corporation, as a source of credit for the export of agricultural products.
Second, why is the Government not taking the lead in attempting to have Poland's debt negotiated by the Paris Club in the same way as that organization or group of countries has dealt with the debts of Brazil, Chile and others? It seems only fair that negotiations should be put in place and spearheaded by Canada, if necessary, to allow that to happen. Farmers would be pleased with anything that would increase the demand for their products. They recognize that part of their responsibility is to feed the world regardless of what President Reagan thinks of the country to which they sell their products and regardless of the ideology which the government of that country has put forward.
Crown corporations in Canada are intended to be instruments of public policy. Their reason for their being is the good
Export Development Act
of the country. If you look at the history of most Crown corporations, particularly when they were set up-and many were set up by previous Conservative Governments-they were set up with a good reason. Many times that reason has disappeared or been cast aside, quite often very shortly after the Crown corporations have gone into business. Instead of operating for the good of the Canadian people, quite often these Crown corporations operate for their own survival. They become so controlled by the bureaucrats put in charge of them that they lose their objective of operating for the good of Canada and start becoming corporations that operate for their own good.
This particular Government has given Crown corporations a very bad reputation, a reputation which is changing public opinion to the extent that many of the ones highly thought of are now in disrepute. Therefore, maybe it is necessary for this Parliament to put some strings on the purses of Crown corporations. A good example of what can happen without referral to Parliament is the late scandal, I suppose we can call it, of Canadair. If it can happen to Canadair-the fact that $1.6 billion in losses were incurred before the corporation was referred back to Parliament-then it can happen to any corporation. Therefore, perhaps it is important that all corporations operate within some restrictions concerning the amount of money they can spend.
Successive Auditors General have indicated quite forcefully and lustily that any money spent anywhere by any corporation, if it is taxpayers' money, must be accounted for in some way to Parliament. We have moved away from this position almost continuously in the last number of years.
Lately, for example, Canadian National Railways, whose reason for being is servicing the transportation industry for all Canadians and whose losses are paid for-made up-by the taxpayers of Canada, has said there is no way the Auditor General, a servant of this Parliament, should be able to look into its books and find out how it lost or made money. The books of the CNR will become very important to the people of Canada, particularly to the farmers of western Canada. If Parliament allows the changes suggested to the Crow rate, the amount of money which will be paid for freight will be directly dependent upon the expenditures of Canadian National Railways. Why should Canadian farmers trust the costing of a company which hides its books from its own people? Why should farmers trust a Government which depends upon a New York economist to tell it how much it costs to operate a company which the Government itself owns? This is what is happening in the refusal by CN to have the Auditor General look into its books. Since the possible successors of the present Government do not have a better record than the present Government, it is necessary to put the restrictions suggested in these amendments on any corporation which spends taxpayers' money.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, we are not speaking today of anything other than establishing a minimum of

parliamentary control over the expenditure of public money. Once again we have the Government coming before Parliament seeking virtually unlimited borrowing power. That is the true meaning of the legislation we are discussing. Once again we are in the position of attempting to curb the Government's ongoing and persistent attempt to remove itself from the fiscal control of Parliament.
The Government has a record of uncontrolled expenditures second to none. Nero in his wildest moments never squandered the public money as this Grit Government has done and is still doing. Now, with the largest deficit in history, the largest public debt in history and the worst financial record since the teapot Dome scandal, it is back again asking for another blank cheque. That is what $20 billion amounts to; that and another $20 billion and yet another $20 billion. If a wage earner made a salary of $20,000 a year, in 100 years that person would earn $2 million. In 1,000 years that wage earner could earn $20 million. In one million years that person could earn $20 billion, a fraction of the authorization for which the Government wants a blank cheque.
1 know it is a hypothetical consideration, particularly under this Government which takes nearly half of what one earns in income and other taxes. Nevertheless, it gives one an idea of the magnitude of the amount with which we are dealing here. But then, this Government always thinks big. If it were in private industry, it would have been in bankruptcy long ago. It has a habit of wheeling and dealing in vast amounts of money, great sprawling schemes and projects and paper programs that never get off the ground. It is a Government that is totally infatuated by its own propaganda.
Day after day the jovial Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) rises and explains that things were never better. He says that we are on the way up. He does not worry about hard facts, such as 1.5 million unemployed Canadians. But then that 1.5 million unemployed Canadians do not vote Grit anyway. Government Members wheel and deal and crank up their propaganda machine to tell Canadians how good they have it. It is fun to be out of work under this Grit Government in its wonderful land of Oz!
For months now the former Minister of Manpower, who is now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy), has been telling Canadians about the hundreds of millions he has been making available in his so-called job-creation programs. Day after day he rose in the House weaving his webs of fantasy. But let me say that if all the jobs in all the paper programs had materialized, not only would there be no one out of work in Canada, but we would be scouring the world for workers. Sadly that is not the case. Unemployment exists, hardship exists, bankruptcies exist. The desperation and uncertainty of young people wondering where they are to turn next is a salient feature of this sagging society, which is the legacy of 15 years of centralization and Government misdirection.
As they go on erecting their castles in the air, spinning their fairy fantasies, one theme is recurrent. They want money, they want more money, they want unlimited money. They are like drunken con artists who, in order to keep their "sting" going,
must constantly attract new sources of supply. New task forces, new consultants, new Government agencies, are spewing forth from the bottomless well of the Government's aimless frittering, demanding always more and more expenditure on the part of the taxpayer who is neither consulted nor asked to approve through his or her elected representative in this place, which is why we are sent here.
The Government must go to the market to borrow something like $25 billion this year in order to finance its day to day operations and to pay interest on its colossal debt. This means overburdening an already tightly stretched money market. It means that interest rates will move up, that ordinary Canadians will be at pains to secure the financing they need, and that once again we will be looking into the yawning maw of recession.
The Minister of Finance has said that this was okay with him, that this was fine with him. He does not want the recovery to be too sudden. He wants Canadians to suffer a little more. He would like to see a few more turns of the screw. Perhaps if Canadians get hungry enough and desperate enough, they will sit back while the Government brings in its Bills to control the press and all the other measures which have the effect of centralizing authority in the Grit Cabinet. This has been its course since resuming office in 1980. It is the course of desperation. It has been a determined and persistent effort by those who want to usher in socialism by the back door, erode the freedoms of Canadians and create a faceless and docile proletariat in the country.
They will find that Canadians are not a mean-spirited people. They will find that Canadians stand up for their rights. They will find that Canadians will not give up their heritage of freedom and independence for a mess of Liberal pottage. Canadians are not prepared to surrender any further authority to this Government of all governments. We are not prepared to give up financial control to a Government and a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who have created in the country a sprawling Frankenstein which was described by the Auditor General as a "parallel government". In the process they have driven this country to the brink of financial insolvency.
The Government is now peddling off our natural resources as quickly as it can to the highest bidders. It is keeping on the special petroleum tax although Petrofina and British Petroleum have been paid for long since. It is holding back on support to the aged and withholding financial support to medicare in order to finance the incredibly costly losses of Canadair and de Havilland and the other tottering fiscal empire under the control of the Prime Minister's friends, Senator Austin and Mr. Bell.
That is where the money is going. That is why we have these incredible deficits. That is why Canada went deeper into recession than any other OECD country and was slower climbing out. That is why Canadians have been forced to accept a reduced standard of living with reduced income. That is why we have placed these amendments before the House.
September 22, 1983

We as Members of Parliament are taking the only recourse open to us to return the control of the public purse to Parliament.
I can tell the Government now how it can get on with this measure so that it can be used as a vehicle to increase our trade with other countries, which after all is the main thrust of the Bill, but with established, traditional parliamentary control. We will give unanimous consent to the restoration of the amendment moved by the Minister, amendment No. 2, if the Government will give unanimous consent to the restoration of our amendment No. 4, which establishes the basic minimum of parliamentary control, and agree to our amendment No. 5. If they are sincere about their respect for the parliamentary tradition, they will accept that offer.
I repeat, we will consent to the re-establishment of the Government's amendment No. 2 if it will consent to the re-establishment of our amendment No. 4 and agree to amendment No. 5. Amendment No. 4 provides for the basic minimum of parliamentary control. That is all we ask, that control remain in the hands of the people through their elected representatives sitting in this House. If that position were to be adopted by the Government, it would have this measure with no further adieu.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order on the point just made by the Hon. Member with regard to a possible deal. Mr. Speaker, I wish to share with the House some thoughts on Bill C-l 10. As my colleague from Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) stated, all we in the Opposition are requesting is control.
In Alberta at the present time we are having municipal, county, school board and hospital board elections. In some cases five, six or seven Members are being elected to various boards. There is heightened activity in my community and in other communities in my riding. Interest in the municipal elections is at an all-time high. Four years ago people vested certain responsibilities in those they elected to represent them on various boards. They now see that in some cases these representatives did not take their job seriously and have not been accountable to the people on how the taxes collected were spent.
I can cite an example without naming the community. There is a hot and heavy campaign going on because the school tax has increased dramatically in the past two years. People see that there has been waste and are calling the school board to account. They believe their tax dollars were collected on a false pretext and have been spent in a frivolous way.
The point 1 am making is that there is accountability at the municipal level. The reason is that their expenditures do not involve megadollars, such as $20 billion, an amount which we continually discuss in this House. The people have a very fair understanding of that. 1, and I am sure no one else in this
Export Development Act
House, can fathom what $20 billion really means. The Hon. Member for Yukon tried to describe it. He said it would take one person earning a normal salary a million years of work to accumulate that amount.
The people who sent me here did so to represent them in the House of Commons. That is the beauty of our system. Each and every Member of this House was sent here with the same mandate. I cannot in good conscience condone what this Government is doing. Through this Bill the Government is asking for a blank cheque, assuming no accountability.
This is not the only place where there is no accountability. All Crown corporations are not accountable to the House of Commons. We do not know how and where money is being spent and whether it is being wasted. I have a theory about why the Government is resisting even the basic minimum accountability for which we are asking.
Yesterday in this House we discussed my motion for the tabling of some documents which would once and for all clear up the issue that arose during the national energy fiasco and the fight with Alberta. 1 asked that those documents be tabled in the House so that Members of my Party, the NDP, the Liberal Party and Canadians from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island could see them. We would know exactly what happened with the Alsands project that was to have taken place in my riding. Because it went down the tube, it is costing this country thousands and thousands of jobs. It is estimated that had those two projects gone ahead, they would have created 500,000 jobs, putting back to work one-third of the unemployed people in this country. The arguments went back and forth and the blame went back and forth. When I asked for unanimous consent for these documents to be placed on the Table, this consent was denied by the Liberal Members.
The same thing is happening here. If the accountability factor that we are suggesting in our amendment is accepted, then the loans, insurance and all the spending that will occur as a result of this Bill would be available for all to see. If all the background material were placed on the Table, everyone would have access to it.
My theory is that the Government does not want the voters across the country to know what is happening with Crown corporations, to know where the money is being spent, how it is being spent and whether it is being spent wisely. I believe it would open up the eyes of all of the voters across the country if they were to see the waste and inefficiency that goes on when the Government is spending dollars that do not belong to it or to its Crown corporations but to the people of Canada. The people of Canada support this institution through their taxes. The Government does not have any money whatsoever; the money belongs to the people of Canada.
1 represent 100,000 of those people in Canada. Each Member in the House of Commons represents basically the same number. That is why we are here, Mr. Speaker. We are here to be accountable and to keep the Government accountable to those people for their money. We are only trustees and

we are placed here by the electorate to keep the Government accountable. The electorate wants to know where its money is being spent and how it is being spent. The people of Canada will never know how that money is being spent if we keep a veil of secrecy around every program to spend money that is developed by the Government.
I urge all Hon. Members to think for a moment about why they were originally elected and why they originally wanted to come to this place to represent the people in their ridings. I am sure that if each Hon. Member were to examine his conscience, he would know that what 1 am saying is true. We must be accountable. We must spend wisely the dollars that are entrusted to us to run the Government.
With that, Mr. Speaker, I would like to close by saying that I do hope that the Hon. Member for Yukon, through his negotiations, will bring sense to this legislation so that we do have that accountability.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in favour of the two motions moved by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), let me echo his sentiments. The issue here is accountability to Parliament. Nobody, I think, knows better than those of us on this side of the House that trade is essential to Canada. Fifty per cent of all the goods produced in our country are exported. An unmeasured quantity of services, such as insurance and banking, are exported. Trade in the form of imports and exports constitutes about 30 per cent of our GNP.
As the Hon. Member for Mississauga South pointed out, though, if this Bill is not amended as we propose, we will be giving the Government $62 billion either by subscription or capital or through loans made by the corporation. As has been said before, we will be allowing the Government to give the Export Development Corporation a blank cheque to do with as it will or as the Government would have it do. That is the reason for our amendments. That is why we have been reduced to putting up speaker after speaker in this debate. It shows how strongly we feel about accountability to Parliament and I suppose it is a sign of the impotence of Parliament that all we as the Opposition can do is put forth speaker after speaker to make ten-minute speeches to show our concern about this fundamental issue of accountability to Parliament.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS IMPORTANCE OF GOVERNMENT'S PRESENCE AT NEXT QUEBEC CITY REGIONAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to express my disapproval of the Quebec Government's decision to refuse to allow representatives of the Government of Canada to take part in the forthcoming summit planned for the Quebec City area. The legendary uptightness of our separatist pequists is once again apparent. Many mayors of our municipalities, commissioners, businessmen and other intervenors are now being blackmailed into taking part in this summit, under the subtle threat of reprisals by our friends in the Quebec Cabinet, the same people who just woke out of their summer stupor to the realization that unemployment is very high in Quebec. Madam Speaker, how can we take this summit seriously if we are not to see the Canadian Government at the consultations that will be held? The presence of the Government of Canada is felt everywhere in the Quebec City area. For instance, the Government's assistance to small, medium-sized and large businesses, the latter including Davie shipyards as the largest industry in the Quebec City area; the federal Public Service, the Port of Quebec, the Societe du Vieux-Port, the Societe Inter Port, Parks Canada with its many facilities, the Quebec City Airport, Transport Canada, the Canadian gas pipeline, and so on.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again the Grit government has fumbled the ball. In its continuing quest for the holy grail of a perfect socialist state it has forgotten about the largest single employer in Canada, an industry providing jobs for more than a million people, representing over 10 per cent of the work force. 1 am speaking of the tourism industry, and the 100,000 tourist establishments and small businesses which accounted for 5 per cent of our GNPin 1982.
This $16 billion a year industry, which generates $4 billion in foreign exchange, is now doing poorly as a direct result of punitive Grit taxation policies. Liquor prices in Canada are 250 per cent higher than those in the U.S., food costs are 50 per cent higher, and tobacco and gas prices are double those south of the border. Federal and provincial Governments spend $80 million a year promoting tourism in Canada, then collect $8 billion in taxes from the industry. That may look like a healthy return on investment, but it is crippling a vital sector of our economy.
September 22, 1983

To add insult to injury, the federal Government promotes Canadian travel abroad. Canadians do not need this encouragement, Madam Speaker. The Liberal approach to tourism is incentive enough for Canadians to travel elsewhere.
The tourism industry is capable of creating more jobs than Liberal make-work programs, but only in a climate which decreases punitive taxation, encourages investment, and allows a profit, not one in which excessive taxation strangles all potential, and increases unemployment.

Madam Speaker, we deplore the remarks of Conservative Senator Richard Donahoe that we would not have the problem of aboriginal rights in Canada "if they did just what they did in Newfoundland and shot them all." The genocide of the Bea-thuk Indians in Newfoundland in the nineteenth century is one of the most shameful atrocities of the European era in Canada. It cannot be the subject of a joke. Genocide is not a subject for humour, not in a world where genocide is a reality and not in a country where injustices to native peoples continue, as seen in appallingly high rates of poverty, unemployment, illness, suicide, and imprisonment of native peoples.
As parliamentarians we must dissociate ourselves from these misguided remarks. Our colleagues working on aboriginal rights must redouble their efforts for a just settlement. The Leader of the Conservative Party has a particular responsibility to throw Senator Donahoe out of caucus and demand his resignation from the Senate. The Hon. Robert Stanfield, when he was Leader of the Conservative Party, refused to allow Leonard Jones to be a member of his caucus. We expect no less of the new Conservative Leader.
Remarks such as Senator Donahoe's, if not the product of racism, reflect a stupidity unacceptable even in a member of an appointed Senate. The first step in Senate reform should be Senator Donahoe's departure. All of Parliament is degraded by his continued membership.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REMOVAL OF HEADQUARTERS FROM NEW YORK TO MONTREAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some of my most memorable events during the years 1961-1965, when 1 worked in New York, were visits to the United Nations. Somehow the entire world is contracted into a few acres where the cries and pleas of effectively all world nations are heard. I was therefore surprised to read U.S. Deputy Ambassador
Charles Lichenstein's remarks that the United Nations would not be missed if it were moved out of New York. In fact he appeared to encourage the prospect of such a move.
Montreal is an excellent site for the United Nations, and Place Ville-Marie would be a suitable temporary accommodation. The Government of Canada should apply itself with diligence to determine the reality of such a relocation, and should let it be known loudly that Canadians would welcome such a relocation.

subsubtopic: PRESERVATION OF BUILDINGS-CALL FOR COMMITTEE STUDY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the issue of heritage and the protection of Canada's historic buildings has become an increasingly important one throughout this year and last. The wanton destruction of the Canadian Pacific West Toronto Station, and more recently the threat of the removal of the historic Essex Railway Station in Mississauga, clearly indicate to many that if we do not find a quick solution to this problem we may well find ourselves without any heritage property and without any recollection of Canada's past.
Many Departments are responsible for our heritage, Departments such as that of the Secretary of State, Environment Canada, Public Works, and Transport Canada. It is time to bring this issue to the forefront. All Departments which have an interest in the heritage question should come together to form an inter-departmental committee to study this issue and draft recommendations and proposed legislation on how to protect the destruction of heritage buildings and to provide for the conservation of buildings of historical or cultural value.

Study after study has recommended that the Government should be considering this proposal, yet the Government makes no decisions on this at a time when there are 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Why is the Government waiting? Technology is here to stay, and Canada is falling behind other countries which have identified this problem, are attacking i,t and creating new policies in conjunction with their business sectors which will encourage retraining, both in the private and public sectors.
In Norway, for example, officials have recognized that technological change involves both problems of unemployment and the retraining of present manpower. In this manner they are able to ensure that private businesses have a sufficient

amount of skilled workers on hand. The costs of this plan would be shared equally by the Government and private enterprise. This, 1 am sure in the long run, would be less costly to all, rather than the alternative of spending billions of dollars on unemployment insurance benefits.

This Act, which affects virtually every Canadian over 16 years of age, has become an instrument of confusion, a document of deception, and a tool of fear and intimidation. The Income Tax Act exists by the will of the Canadian people and yet, in the hands of this Government, it has become a vehicle of control.
September 22, 1983

In the Government's budget of 1980-81 the Government introduced 350 changes. When the author of that budget flopped and a new one flipped in, he introduced a further 133 amendments which have contributed further to this complexity which can best be described by example.
Section 39, the definition of capital gains, begins with one sentence consisting of two semicolons, 28 commas, and, believe it or not, 774 words. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and on behalf of all members of our caucus and our members and supporters across the country, we pay tribute today to the memory of Andrew Brewin, the former Member of Parliament for Greenwood. To his wife Peggy, his son John and his daughters Margaret, Martha, Mary and Jane and other members of his family, we extend our deepest sympathy.
Andrew Brewin was one of our most distinguished former Members and his passing has deprived Canada of a man of passionate commitment toward the eradication of injustice in our world.
Andrew Brewin first won election to the House of Commons in 1962 and he won re-election until his retirement in 1979. In the years he served the House and the country, his concern for the wellbeing of his constituents was always at the forefront of his actions as he pressed for resolutions to their problems. For that he earned the respect of the people in Greenwood and the admiration and friendship of his constituents.
The Late Andrew Brewin
Andrew Brewin was a man who devoted his whole adult life to the service of others. He was a man of ideas and conscience and it was here in this House that he was able to speak to Canadians day in and day out about social and economic justice, about the gap between the rich and the poor and about the crying need in our world for a greater understanding between its peoples.
Andrew Brewin was a man who was devoted to work always for the common good. It was this devotion that convinced him to take up the case of Japanese Canadians who were so unjustly treated at the beginning of the Second World War. It was because of that devotion that he fought against injustice not only in Canada but internationally as well. He argued tenaciously on behalf of the needs of people in developing nations and about the obligation of the developed countries to give greater assistance to those areas.
Even after he left this House, Madam Speaker, Andrew Brewin continued to be an outspoken advocate for those principles he profoundly believed in. His lifelong work which was dedicated toward achieving world peace was well known to Members of the House, and over the past several years he increased those efforts against what he termed as the insanity in the growth of nuclear armaments.
In voicing his compassion, Andrew Brewin was always civilized and advanced his arguments with reason and warmth. It was Andrew Brewin's force and conviction that brought me and many others that I know of into active politics and the example that he set will live on long after his passing.
Andrew Brewin was a great Canadian and a great humanitarian. His work in this House and internationally is his legacy to our great country. We will all miss him.

Member for Greenwood came to this House and who was also here when he left the House, 1 would like to associate the Official Opposition with the remarks that have been made by the Hon. Those of us who knew Andrew Brewin recognized his dedication to and concern for others. We recognized his consuming interest in securing justice for the dispossessed and the underprivileged. Those views were a credit to his Party and to the country as a whole.
He was a very able Parliamentarian, always sincere and straightforward with no guile or deviousness in his nature or in his soul. He fought very strongly for the things in which he believed and afterwards, as the Hon. Minister has just said, he was always ready to extend a hand in friendship to his colleagues in the House.
He was a member of the New Democratic Party at a time when some of its Members were giants in the House. T. C. Douglas, David Lewis, and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is still with us, lent lustre to the Chamber.
The late Hon. Member for Greenwood was always in the forefront of debate, putting forward his Party's position with grace, dignity and moderation. He always had a good word for the argument of an opponent and, while prepared to uphold his views with competence and very often with wit, could always see good in the opinions of others.
He was one of those people who went to Africa over a decade ago to obtain first-hand information on conditions on that troubled continent.
He was a Parliamentarian in every sense of the word with a true love of this Chamber and a true respect for its traditions.
He knew what Parliament was about and was aware of the insoluble link between the right of free expression and the preservation of our liberties.
The sympathy of Members of this Party goes to his colleagues and to his family, i say sincerely on behalf of all of us in this Party that he will be missed.

I also know his wife, Peggy, very well and his five children, one son and four daughters. They are all married, I was at their weddings and I have had connections with them in various other ways. We are very appreciative of the kind of people the Brewins are and of the personal friendships we have had together. I welcome this opportunity in Parliament to remember his wife, children and grandchildren and we extend to them our very best wishes.
1 am grateful for what other Members have said, both on behalf of this Party and the Liberal and Conservative Parties. They spoke of the breadth of his interest. He was a strong and active politician and was greatly concerned about certain matters. While he was interested in international affairs, world relations and that sort of thing, he also visited other countries of the world because he wanted to render any service he could in helping to make life better for other people. He was concerned about relations in this country, about our Constitution and the things that affect people in a place such as the City of Toronto. He played a very important role.
