Madam Speaker, when the House recessed at one o'clock l was in the process of discussing the implications of taking from the House of Commons and placing in to the hands of the board of directors of a Crown corporation the significant judgment which has to be made with respect to the making of loans and the consequences thereof.
This becomes very important when one examines the way in which these funds which are loaned by the Export Development Corporation are treated in their financial statement. I have before me the most recent set of financial statements, with notes attached thereto, which form part of the Annual Report for the year ended December 31, 1982. It is of particular interest to find when you note the statement of assets that a total net advance by way of principal loan receivables amounts to $4,5 billion, roughly, with respect to which there is a reserve for what is referred to as "losses on loans" of $53 million. That is a reserve for losses which have not as yet been realized.
With respect to the loan guarantees and the interest earned, an examination of the financial statements will show that there is a $6 million reserve against loan guarantees outstanding in the amount of $404 million, roughly. I was curious as to why the amount of intended reserves should be so little, having regard to the very substantial quantum of outstanding loans. The answers are very clear and are explained by way of notes in the financial statement. They are rather elaborate, but I believe I have enough time to put them on the record. Let me read from page 25 of the Annual Report:
The provision for losses on loans is based on a review of collectibility of all outstanding loans to sovereign and commercial borrowers. In respect of this review, the Corporation recognizes that the future economic and political conditions in some of the countries where the Corporation has made loans are

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
subject to varying degrees of pressures, some of which are unpredictable. Accordingly, delays in the repayment of principal and interest may well occur from lime to time.
In the case of loans made to sovereign borrowers, that is the governments of countries or their agencies, payment delays are not necessarily indicative of a future loss requiring a provision. Sovereign entities and their international financial obligations do not have commercial mortality, and the international system does not allow the unilateral denial of a sovereign obligation. Furthermore, the international system provides several mechanisms and institutions through which countries facing repayment difficulties can effect remedial measures in agreement with their creditors. Therefore, except in the rare instance of outright repudiation or a write-off of asset value agreed to by creditors, in the opinion of management the ultimate collectibility of a sovereign obligation, and thus its asset value, is not subject to question, although delays may have to be accepted.
It is the policy of the Corporation to set aside from net income, in addition to any specific provisions made as a result of the review of the outstanding loans, an amount sufficient to maintain an accumulated non-specific allowance proportionate to the total loan principal and interest receivable for which no specific provision has been made.
What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is a complete repudiation of the general principles which apply in the case of commercial loans made by the private sector, and it is something which should alarm the general public. The statement here flies in the face of the fact that a nation like North Korea, when it suited it, completely repudiated the obligations which it had to the international community. And it is a true fact that as long as the lender in any situation, be it international or local, continues to advance money to the borrower, that loan will never be bad; it is uncollectable only when the loan is called.
What this note to the financial statement indicates very clearly is that the usual considerations which apply when examining whether a loan is a bad loan with respect to which a reserve should be claimed or not, are not listened to or paid attention to, on the false premise that sovereign powers are immortal. That is a strange justification, Mr. Speaker, because very clearly if a loan is made for SI00 million and advanced for a period of 50 years interest-free, and this House has no opportunity of determining exactly what the terms of those loans are, the value of that loan in the financial statements of this Crown corporation can clearly be zero, particularly when the recipient of those funds happens to be a nation which may be hostile to Canada.
My great concern and the concern of my colleagues has been expressed throughout this debate. We have no opportunity to deal with these substantive issues when the very matters with respect to which I direct the attention of the House are taken out of the House and transferred to a board of directors who will now be made up exclusively of members of the senior Public Service in Canada. That will be the situation if the Bill in its present form goes through as requested by the Government.
One thing we should also pay some attention to is the growth within the public sector of Government expenditure as a portion of the GNP of this nation. That growth today stands at 49.2 per cent of the GNP. If this corporation uses the powers granted to it under this Bill and in fact borrows the $20 billion to which reference has been made, that will have two
very substantial effects on the business community. It will dry up the available funds for regular commercial activities and force up interest rates, the very things this Government tells us it wishes not to do.
Thank you Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I think I am about the one hundredth speaker on Bill C-l 10.
One hundred and one.

1 guess you have to ask yourself why we are fielding 101 speakers on this Bill. 1 have not been able to find more than a squib on it in the newspapers ever since we started debating the Bill. Certainly the media does not care very much about it and probably most of the Canadian public does not understand the Bill. So why in the world would 101 Members of Parliament stand up in this House of Commons and fight so fiercely this particular legislation?
It is not a very significant piece of legislation. It only enables the Government to go out and put at risk $62 billion of taxpayers' hard-earned money. It is not really all that significant, I suppose. So why are we fighting so hard over a paltry $62 billion? Mr. Speaker, the reason we are fighting so hard on this Bill and why we are going to continue to fight so hard is because we are fighting against the Government's intransigence, its unwillingness to introduce any semblance of accountability to this institution. What we are fighting for in this Bill is this institution. What is the purpose of our being here if we are all totally irrelevant? I include in that the backbenchers of the Liberal Party as well as the Opposition Party. What is the point of being here if we are simply a rubber stamp to be tramped on by the Government at will? That is what this legislation is all about.
We have asked for just a few amendments to this Bill to give Parliament just a little wee bit of say over how the Government might want to spend $62 billion of the Canadian taxpayers' money. All we have asked for is some semblance of representation on the board of directors to introduce some responsibility, accountability and control over the management of the Export Development Corporation. But no, that is to be denied us.
Why is it that the Government does not want to do anything about amending Bill C-l 10? Why is it that for the last seven years Crown corporations have been a subject of debate? There is a mountain of information about the management, control and accountability, the role and responsibilities of directors of Crown corporations. Yet the Government does not know anything about it. It just turns its back. Not one thing has been done about it. You can go back to the Lambert Commission and the reports of J. J. Macdonell, the Auditor General who preceded Mr. Kenneth Dye, and Mr. Henderson who preceded Mr. Macdonell. Consistently, year after year after year, they have reported that Crown corporations are poorly managed, indeed out of control.
I would like to read you something, Mr. Speaker, written by a gentleman who shall remain unnamed but who has spent
September 22, 1983

most of his life in Government administering Crown corporations. He says that unfortunately the Crown corporation concept is in deep trouble, it is a very good idea that is badly abused, he says. By and large most of the Crown corporations are poorly managed, drawing on Government money as if it were a bottomless pit. They have Ministers who do not know what they are doing, and boards of directors stacked with patronage appointments. I guess nothing more clearly exemplifies what this gentleman is saying than the disaster, the catastrophe of Canadair.
But to come back to my point, Mr. Speaker, why does the Government not want to do anything about these Crown corporations'? Why does it not want to introduce into this House legislation to put some teeth into the management, control and accountability of Crown corporations? You have to ask yourself why. Why does the Government not want to do it, Mr. Speaker? There must be a reason why. You have a blue ribbon commission headed by Mr. Lambert and successive Auditors General who have clearly stated the need for reform. You have the members of the Business Council on National Issues who have pleaded with the Government to introduce reform. When we were in government we introduced Bill C-27, and the Liberals stonewalled it. Then the Government comes back with its own version of reform in Bill C-153, which really is simply a fraud and window-dressing, as evidenced by the fact that the other side has withdrawn the Bill.
So, Mr. Speaker, what is at the heart of the government's desire to not want to proceed with these reforms? Well, to do so would detract from the Liberal Government's ability to manipulate for their own political advantage. These Crown corporations cost the Canadian people in 1981-82 some $6.5 billion. Most people, including myself, cannot even get their arms around a billion, let alone six and a half of them. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, $6.5 billion. But no, this Government refused to introduce any reforms for the benefit of Canadians because it would interfere with political patronage and political manipulation for their benefit. I can think of no better way to illustrate this point than by giving you two examples. Sometime in the next little while we are going to see what is called the Canada Development Investment Corporation, the CDIC. It will be capitalized at the small amount of $3 billion. But it is going to have control of Canadair, de Havilland, Teleglobe, and it will acquire the share of Government ownership in the Canada Development Corporation which controls Texas Gulf Sulphur and many other companies.
We are told that the purpose of the CDIC is to enable us to manage properly the assets of these other Crown corporations. Why? Because a management team has been put in place that knows how to deal with all of these problems. At its head is Senator Jack Austin. Then there is the infamous Mr. Maurice Strong, who certainly qualifies as a great manager, there is no question. He is a Liberal so he must be a good manager. Then there is the architect of the National Energy Program, Mr. Joel Bell. These gentlemen will do all these good things for Canadians and will manage this $3 billion monster corporation. Not only are we told that they will manage it properly,
Export Development Act
CDIC will look after the interests of the taxpayers of Canada by disposing of those assets that can be managed more properly by the private sector. These gentlemen have never sold anything in their lives.
The CDIC is a blatant instrument of further state intervention, and no Canadian should misunderstand its purpose. Anything else that one hears is tommyrot, and that Government knows it but does not have the courage to stand up and admit the truth. When we say more state intervention, what does it mean to most people? Canadians like to think that we have a wonderful blend or mix in Canada of state intervention and private enterprise. They assume we get along very well this way and that Canada has this unique situation where it has a little bit of each and that we get along fine with state intervention.
Since I am running out of time I will try to wrap up very quickly. People do not seem to understand what is at stake here, and the Government certainly does not want them to understand. Jobs are at stake and that is what we are concerned about. We are talking about jobs. State intervention means the loss of jobs and the loss of the ability of Canada's economy to compete in the real world today. We will never create jobs in Canada until we are prepared to face international competition. There is no commodity for which Canada sets the price. We are at the mercy of prices for every single thing out in the real world.
State intervention represents a misallocation of capital. That $6.5 billion which I referred to a few moments ago could perhaps create 100,000 jobs for Canadians who are unemployed in this country today. Canadians will be faced with a very clear choice in a few years from now. That choice is whether they want jobs or further Government intervention in their lives and more agencies like CDIC. Crown corporations are depriving Canadians of their jobs. They are depriving us of the motivation, innovation and willingness to adapt to the real world. Canada represents less than one-half of one per cent of the world population. If we believe that we can win the battle in international markets of the world through Crown corporations we are very sadly mistaken.

Mr. Speaker, 1 had not intended to participate in this debate and 1 do not intend to make a long speech at this time. I will agree with my friends in the Conservative Party about the incompetent manner in which the Liberal Government has managed Crown corporations.
However, it does seem to me that some Members from the Conservative Party should deal more honestly with the whole question of Crown corporations than the Hon. Member who just finished speaking. Crown corporations in Canada are not the creation of the federal Liberal Government, they are in existence in every Province of this country, and they have been created by Conservative federal Governments as well.

While I will not go through the entire list, in my Province there is a publicly owned provincial telephone system which was established in 1908. It was not established by some socialist government but by the Conservative Government of the day headed by Sir Rodmond Roblin, the grandfather of Senator Roblin. There is a provincially owned telephone system in the Province of Saskatchewan which I believe was established by a Liberal Government. A great example of a Crown corporation in this Province is Ontario Hydro. It was established by a Conservative Government and has been managed by a Conservative Government which has been in power continuously for the last 40 years. The present Ontario Government purchased a substantial share in Sun Oil over a year ago. I could go on, but the point 1 am making is that Crown corporations are not foreign and not something foisted on the Canadian people by a Liberal Government alone.
Crown corporations have a long history in Canada. Most of them have an honourable history. They have been established by federal and provincial Governments, Liberal, Conservative, NDP or indeed Social Credit. It seems to me that it was the Social Credit Government in British Columbia which took over the hydro-electric system and made it a public utility owned by the people.
Crown corporations have been established in this country for many years. They were established because a government, whether Liberal, Conservative, NDP or Social Credit, believed that the private sector was not prepared to do what was necessary. I remind the Hon. Member who just spoke that it was a Conservative Government in Ottawa which established the Canadian Wheat Board and a Conservative Government in Ottawa which established the CBC. That is the reality.
While 1 agree with many of the criticisms made by my friends in the Conservative Party about how the Government operates and manages Crown corporations-and certainly one of the worst examples of how to do things is the establishment of the Canadian Development Investment Corporation-I wish that at least one Conservative Member of Parliament would try to tell us honestly whether they believe there is a role for any Crown corporation or whether they really believe, like some of the Reagonite and Goldwater Republicans in the U.S., that the Government should do less and less and that almost everything should be left to the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, it makes sense to hear my friend from the NDP defending Crown corporations because they take the attitude that they would like everything owned by the Government. They would like pure socialism. We would be in the same situation as the Russians.
1 believe that this Bill is nothing more than proliferation of subgovernment. The Liberal Party is requesting permission to go out and literally spend an extra $34 billion. The Government is asking for an unbelievable amount of money to give to foreign countries to buy our products. Anyone who has any basic knowledge of economics knows that one cannot give everything away for nothing and then borrow and leave it in a financial statement. Let me refer to state to state loans. Poland has a state to state loan. This is shown in their financial
statements. We questioned the Auditor General. We asked why we did not write that loan off and be honest. Instead the Government capitalizes the interest on that loan ad infinitum. It is time we faced up to our losses, wrote them off and got on with managing this country properly. An example of that under Crown corporations is the CDIC. It took Canadair over through a very bad time. We as a Government have written off $2 billion to develop a toy, an executive jet. It may be a very fine product. But now we turn it over to CDIC. It cannot help but make money out of it. Believe me, the way Crown corporations in this country operate, the CDIC will blow it. The CDIC is incapable of selling the product because there is no incentive in the bureaucracy. We seem to proliferate Crown corporations. What is interesting about CDIC is that the Minister in charge is the Minister of Social Development. If the Government had taken that $2 billion, it could have retired every employee of Canadair on $60,000 a year indexed. That is social development, not running a company into the ground.
Furthermore, this is a political ploy on the part of the Liberal Party. It picks a Minister who is in the other place and says he is in charge of CDIC. I checked back with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. That Department is still involved. Why does the Government not face up to it and put the responsibility for CDIC where it belongs, that is with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr, Lumley), let him answer questions in the House, which we have still not had answered in committee, and face up to the problem facing this country?
Another example concerning a Crown corporation which really upset me this week was when the Chairman of Canadian National, a great Canadian citizen, stood up and said the Auditor General should not meddle in the affairs of CNR. He is covering up. The Chairman is frightened to have the Auditor General deal with his financial statements. We need a comprehensive audit on every Crown corporation in Canada. We must start winding up Crown corporations. Crown corporations should only be started where the private sector is not capable of providing capital to get a corporation going. But we should not continue operating them. I would say the CBC is a prime example. It has proceeded from being a moderate organization to costing the taxpayers of Canada very close to $1 billion a year. I can watch many programs on the CBC on an American network by way of cable. I believe the original concept of the CBC, as for Canadian National and for Air Canada, is very sound. Because of the length and breadth of this country, we had to subsidize communication and transportation to help Canadians. Once we do that and we get these entities on their feet, they should be turned over to the private sector.
With respect to the private sector, the Economic Council of Canada in its report clearly states that the EDC should be reduced, restricted and its function should be taken over by the private sector. The American Credit Insurance Corporation does about ten times the volume of business the EDC does. That corporation or another credit corporation could handle
September 22, 1983

this business if it were assisted on these difficult state to state loans. I will acknowledge there are some state to state loans that must be made because we have a responsibility to the Third World. But why do we not face up to these responsibilities to the Third World and write off these loans after we have made them?
We object to this Bill, Mr. Speaker. The Government is asking us as representatives of the Canadian public to triple in Clause 14 and quadruple in Clause 18 the potential available cash that would be taken out of the taxpayers' pockets. There is not enough revenue coming into the Government to handle this kind of expenditure. Our request is very simple. We say that when a Crown corporation needs funds, it should come before the House, explain the purpose of the funds and have the matter debated by the representatives of the Canadian public. We would not be doing our job in the House, we would not be representing our constituencies, and I would not be representing the voters in the constituency of Ontario if I did not speak violently against this type of proliferation and permission to borrow. This should not be allowed.
The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has said, "We will do a deal. We will reduce the amount." That still is not good enough. The Government must come to this Parliament at least twice a year if it wants to spend this kind of money. The Government must come to Parliament and request the funds and tell us the purpose for the funds. I do not mean to put a total roadblock in front of the Government. We do not want the Liberals to do the same thing to us when we become the Government within the next year or so. 1 would not want that kind of roadblock. There must be some flexibility. But $34 billion is an awful lot of flexibility. It is about one-fifth of our total national debt. That means increasing our national debt by another 20 per cent. This country cannot afford any more deficits. It is having crippling effects on industry; the service industry and the tourist industry.
For example, let us take a look at the tourist industry. Through taxation programs, tax on gasoline and tax on liquor, it is driving tourists out of the country. As a result, we are $1.2 billion in the red. I hear the explanation from the Liberals that "Our people like to get the sun in the winter time." There are many Canadians who not only get the sun but who go to ski in areas run by private enterprise in the United States because we are not assisting our tourist industry here in Canada, particularly the ski industry.
I think this whole Bill has to be rewritten. 1 think the Economic Council of Canada, a very responsible organization, has stated it very clearly. This Bill should be withdrawn by the Government and it should be redrawn. The Government should take into consideration some of the points we have made and bring the Bill back to the House, possibly after the next Throne Speech.

Mr. Speaker, the first thing I would like to do is to accept the challenge of my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and tell him yes, there is the odd good Crown corporation. In fact,
Export Development Act
when I become Prime Minister I will make the NDP a Crown corporation and then privatize it.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

With no tongue in check this time let me say that, quite naturally, there are corporations which serve the public well, but that is not what this debate is all about. This is a debate about accountability. We have a Government today which is writing a cheque and signing it without filling in the numbers. It is being printed on latex and extended to the Export Development Corporation for a period of ten years, allowing that corporation to spend up to $62 billion without telling Canadians what the money is to be used for, how it is to be spent or when it will be spent. We live in a democratic country where the people, through this institution, are supposed to control the king's purse.
As Opposition Members we are responding to why Members of Parliament are here in the first place, that is, to control expenditures which are made on behalf of Canadian taxpayers. There is no piece of legislation as fundamental as the one with which we are dealing today. Canadians all across the country are deeply concerned about the enormous growth of Government expenditures. Its spending is out of control, and we are in a situation today of being partially shock-insulated. The average citizen does not know what a billion dollars is. A dollar bill is exactly six inches in length, so two of them make a foot. A billion dollars placed end to end in dollar bills will stretch from Halifax to Vancouver and back two and a half times. The Government wants the authority to take 62 of those without any accountability to Canadians. A former Cabinet Minister of the present Government, now the Chairman of CN and unfortunately a constituent of mine, is now saying that the Auditor General should keep his nose out of the auditing of any Crown corporation. The fact of the matter is that Canadians are begging to know where their money is being spent. I accept the challenge of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North. It is not a question of whether or not each and every Crown corporation fits on a scale of good or bad. It is a question of what this place is for. This place should provide the Government with an opportunity to respond to how people's moneys are being spent.
I would like to do something today which, I concede at the outset, is somewhat unfair. I will refer to some examples of Government expenditures that are obviously wasteful. While Canadians will understand them easily and readily, they really do not add up to all that much in terms of a percentage of total Government waste. However, I want to illustrate that this kind of legislation is an example of the willy-nilly non-accountability of Government. There is an attitude filtering through the Public Service that if it is taxation money, it does not matter. Let me turn to these examples of expenditures which seem to grow like Topsy in the back of the barnyard.

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
Some years ago the Anti-Inflation Board was established. The then Minister of Finance, Donald Macdonald, said that he would require a staff of fewer than 200 persons. Before the year was up, his staff numbered 866 persons, with a salary tab in excess of $ 15 million annually. That is simply an example of what happens throughout the country. We live in the world of language where repeated Ministers of Finance have talked about the principal objective of getting inflation and unemployment under control, yet we continue to be faced with the Government seeking authority for $62 billion without accountability, with no time period for spending the money, and without returning to Parliament. During the first term of office of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), Edgar Benson, the then Minister of Finance, said that his budget was intended to show that they really meant business in their fight against inflation. That was in 1969. Then in 1973, the first budget of John Turner indicated that its purpose first and foremost was to bring about a substantial reduction in unemployment. Then in the second budget of John Turner in 1974, he indicated that it reflected his determination to deal with inflation. This was followed by the budget of Donald Macdonald who indicated that their goals were clear and that their first objective was to maintain underlying trends to lower inflation. Then we come to the budget of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) who expected inflation to be down by the end of the year. Then the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) brought in a couple of glorious budgets which woke up the country. Now the good gentleman over there, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), tells us that we are in a beautiful economic period of time. I am sure there are two million Canadians who do not agree with him.
It is this kind of non-accountability which makes 67 per cent of respondents indicate in the Gallup poll that they do not believe this institution is relevant. They do not believe there is any accountability. We used to have representative democracy where people could elect a Member of Parliament to come here, to speak on their behalf and to talk about the control of money. This place has gone wild. They are asking us to appropriate. The Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, has been telling us that we have to be careful of appropriation of more and more money to Crown corporations and of having a sub-layer of Government gone wild.
I would like to return to the examples of Government expenditure which were discovered by the Auditor General a few years ago. He indicated that the Army had a supply of overalls to last 97 years, that the Air Force had enough light bulbs for 250 years, and that the Navy had underwear of a particular size which would meet its requirements for 1,000 years.
They were not Stanfield.

No, they were not Stanfield. Had they been, we might have had a better Armed Forces today. Then there was the example of a piece of aircraft navigational equipment which cost $9,000 and had a replacement value of $15,000. It
was sent to be repaired and was declared surplus in error and sold for $20. I warned Hon. Members that these examples would be somewhat unfair, but they are little examples which people understand when the Government is requesting $62 billion in Bill C-110. They make public servants believe that when there is no accountability in this forum they do not have to be accountable in their own forum.
In the mid 1960s the Post Office Department overestimated the volume of Christmas mail. The result was that there were 53 million Christmas stamps, at a printing cost of $16,000, which were of no use after that season. The defence Department agreed to pay 25 cents per cubic foot for gas at Camp Wainwright in Alberta, although its contract was for only 21 cents. Over the years, the Department of Public Works has had its fair share of criticism because of waste and mismanagement. A firm of architectural engineers was paid $13,000 for plans to erect a two-storey federal building in Kelowna, British Columbia. Subsequently, the plans were useless because the Government decided to build a four-storey structure. An architectural firm was paid $15,000 to design the four-storey building, but once again the Government changed its mind, decided to build a three-storey structure, and the plans for the four-storey structure were also put in the waste bucket.
If we in this place cannot be accountable for the waste of some $62 billion without accountability, signing over latex cheques to EDC, surely these little examples that haunt Canadians, because they understand the size of numbers, it is only natural that we are not showing leadership here.
Order please. 1 regret to interrupt the Hon. Member, but his time has expired. The Hon. Member may continue his remarks with unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) was not given the opportunity to continue his remarks. They were very pointed and made a strong case with regard to our concerns over this Bill.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-110.
1 once again refer to the clause we are debating today, particularly the part amended by my colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). It begins this way:
-from which outstanding contingent liabilities of the Corporation to which the arrangement applies are directly or indirectly derived ... shall not at any time exceed ten billion dollars.
That is the way the present Bill reads. The amendment put forward by my colleague is that it "shall not at any time exceed 3 billion 500 million and 1". The whole purpose of what we are trying to address in this debate and with this piece of legislation is not so much the money but the concept or the
September 22, 1983

feeling about what has been happening to Parliament and to the country with legislation brought forward by this Government over the last few years.
There is no doubt that all of us recognize that this is a very complex time. The issues we are faced with on a daily basis are extremely complex. The responsibilities that we as individuals carry, whether as Members of Parliament, business people or in some other walk of life, are very complex. That complexitity encourages us to seek out expertise, to go to people who are experts in a given area.
That is the same situation that we have had over the last few years in terms of Government and of legislation and specifically what we see in cases like this. Once you proceed to obtaining experts, the next step is to allow those experts to come together to form a bureaucracy. Up until that point it is not too bad. However, the next step is that the bureaucrats, that group of experts, suddenly has to pass regulations. At that point, we as Parliamentarians have to become very careful and watch what is happening, because we then begin to see the serious situation that is demonstrated by what this Government has put forward in Bill C-110.
Once the bureaucracy begins to pass regulations, it also begins to centralize its own authority. The authority collected through that agency is authority that is taken away from Parliament. That becomes very significant when you are dealing with Crown corporations and Government agencies that deal with, use and spend taxpayer's money. What is important is that every time you have taxpayer's money being used, that money should be overseen, watched by those who have been elected by the taxpayers.
Once you have all of this centralized authority, you have essentially the authority of Parliament, the watchdogs for the taxpayer. That responsibility goes on down the line, and that lack of responsibility is transferred down from segment to segment. If it is allowed to go on long enough, it almost brings you to the point where you have taxation without representation. We know what kind of revolt that has caused in the past.
The problem, even on the very smallest scale, is that you end up with a lack of service to those people intended to be served, the taxpayers, those who pay the taxes. They have elected us to represent them and to demonstrate their concerns to the Government. We are to have an input into what kind of legislation is put forward. Because of this evolution and because the authority of a Member of Parliament has been reduced, a very difficult situation has developed. That is exactly what Bill C-110 is all about and why we have to introduce amendments such as those brought forward by my colleague.
The question is whether we can change what has been happening. 1 think we can. In fact, I think we have to. 1 wish to quote from an article in the Edmonton Journal of September 18 which demonstrates the kind of situation we are dealing with. It reads:
Cabinet has passed 2.789 orders in council-laws and expenditures passed by cabinet behind closed doors-since January I. The orders do not need parliamentary approval nor are they referred to MPs for debate. They come into effect
Export Development Act
after a mere flick of the prime minister's pen. In contrast, the House of Commons considered 49 bills during that period. Only 29 gained approval. Can there be any doubt where the real power lies in Ottawa?
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau must carry a lot of blame for making Parliament irrelevant. What is relevant is a powerful political machine, which includes senior bureaucrats and top cabinet ministers, he set up in his office. But the blame is not entirely his to bear-Parliament allowed it to happen.
There is a lot of truth in that article. No doubt Parliament has allowed this kind of thing to happen. That is why we must take a stand on such Bills as Bill C-110. If this is allowed to continue as it has in the past, it will continue to erode the authority of Parliament, transferring the authority from here to Crown corporations, departments and bureaucracies, anywhere but into the hands of elected officials and those called upon to represent Canadians.
The big question is how to solve the problem. We are doing that today by introducing amendments such as this. The question is whether the Government Members and Government backbenchers who are equally responsible to their constituents, will recognize what they are doing by transferring their authority from Parliament to the Crown corporations. This question must be addressed seriously.
1 have been a member of the committee on procedural reform. John Holtby, an adviser to the committee, recently gave me the results of the poll regarding the opinion of Canadians on the relevance of Parliament. It indicates what they think of Parliamentarians and what they think of Parliament as an institution. This has been talked about lately in the press. There have been various comments on it. There is no doubt that Canadians do not see this institution as relevant. They are not concerned about the relevance of Members because more and more what the Member says, does and controls is becoming severely limited. This is not being done on a grand scale. It is not something we suddently realize. There is no flash of lightening that strikes and indicates that this must be stopped. There has been a constant erosion for more than a decade. Since 1968, the authority of Parliament has been whittled away, some of it going to the Crown corporations, some to the bureaucracy. It is always transferred away from the elected Member of Parliament and this institution. The net result is what we see coming out of recent polls.
The Government has speeded up the process. It has encouraged it through Orders in Council, through legislation which allows so much bureaucratic control and so much discretion, and through the vast use of regulations. Anyone who has seen some of the energy Bills recently passed in the House would be frightened by the regulations attached to that legislation and the authority that is in place for those regulations.
It is a serious issue, Mr. Speaker, and it is not simply one of changing the figure from $10 billion to $3,500 million. It is the whole issue of who is responsible to whom. As we as elected officials must realize and must demonstrate and must do all we can to protect that authority, it must remain in Parliament. Therefore, we must go through with amendments to legislation

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
such as this. As long as the Government continues to bring in bad legislation that can harm Canadians in such a way, we as the Opposition will have no choice but to stand up, Member after Member, to speak to this very important issue.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. Owing to the great many Hon. Members on our side who have wanted to be on record concerning accountability in this type of legislation, this is the first opportunity I have had to speak on this subject.
The Chair will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the general thrust of Bill C-l 10 is to expand the operational capacity of the Export Development Corporation. The objection our Party has to this particular legislation is to the way that the Government wants to do this, and that is, without any further reference to Parliament and without any further need for paid-up capital. We now feel, and have always felt, that it is the job of all Crown corporations to be accountable to the Members of Parliament who represent the taxpayers who are funnelling the money into these Crown corporations.
The second thrust of the Bill is naturally to allow the Government to make more political appointments of Grits to the board of directors of operations such as the Export Development Corporation. We on our side understand that it is necessary to pay people to be Grits and to occupy those positions because it is so difficult to be a Grit these days. If a person can get free trips to attend board meetings to sit as a board member, fine, why not? That is the second thrust of the Bill.
What we are concerned about, however, is the very essence of the difference between the approach taken by the two major Parties in the country to accountability. It is the policy of the Progressive Conservative Party that Crown corporations be accountable to Parliament. It is the policy of the Liberal Government to set up the Crown corporations, give them as much money as they want in the form of a carte blanche, appoint a Grit board of directors and send them on their way. They can come back every so often for more money, but the basic idea is to get out there and spend money. The Government does not want Crown corporations to be accountable.
I refer the Chair to the recent speech made by the late great Jack Horner, a man who went to his political reward as the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Canadian National-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: He's not a long-time Grit.

Yes, he has obviously overcome that, and one might say that he has gone down very fast. Now he executes the office of Chairman of the Board of Directors of Canadian National by running around the country making speeches in which he says to the Auditor General, the independent representative of the Parliament of Canada, "Keep your nose out of our business".
The Chairman has obviously missed the point of the function of the Auditor General. The Auditor General's function is not to determine whether the policy is correct. That is our job. Once a policy is passed by the House of Commons, we
appreciate that, whether we like it or not, that policy is not within the ambit of the Auditor General. It is within the ambit of the Auditor General to make sure that Canadian taxpayers get fair value for their money, that the administration of the taxpayers' dollars through Crown corporations is carried out with an efficiency that gives value for money. That is what the Auditor General is interested in.
The Chairman of Canadian National puts up a specious argument by saying, "Well, our internal auditors who report to our board of directors tell us whether or not it is being done properly." He obviously does not appreciate the difference between an internal auditor from a firm of independent chartered accountants and the Auditor General. We understand that. We had a fair bit to do with him when he was on this side of the House and we understand his deficiencies in appreciating those differences.
I was pleased that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), made mention of the remarks of that great saver of the Canadian taxpayers' dollar, the former Finance Minister, John Turner. He is known affectionately as "Old Blue Eyes", the man who waits in his corporate law office on Bay Street to come and save the Canadian public from the mess that the present Government has got them into.
1 know that there are many people on that side of the House who wait for him with great interest, such as, for example, the new Minister of State responsible for Small Business who is to be a sort of paid watchdog for "Old Blue Eyes" when he comes back to the House on his white steed in his "second coming", as it were, to save the country.
I do know that many of us on this side of the House would welcome the reappearance of "Old Blue Eyes". Anyone who practises law in a county town can hardly wait to get his hands on a Bay Street lawyer, so he can come any time he wants. He could tell us that the purpose of the next budget, first and foremost, will be to bring about a substantial reduction in unemployment. We would welcome that today because the present minister of unemployment-I am sorry, 1 said unemployment when I meant finance.
It is the same thing.

It is actually the same thing. He has nothing to offer to ease unemployment. As a matter of fact, his idea is just to spread unemployment around.
I would like to refer directly to Motions Nos. 6 and 8. Bill C-l 10 would give the Cabinet the right to make its own decisions above and beyond those of the Liberal board of directors of the EDC. With these motions, we are trying to cut back on what Cabinet can do to override the moves of the board of directors.
You will know, Mr. Speaker, that the House has seen other examples of Cabinet operations where the Cabinet decides how things will happen. There is, for example, the Maislin situation where, because of the friendship between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Bronfman family, it was decided that Maislin would get a $34 million loan guarantee. That set a bit of a precedent because the Government had
September 22, 1983

never guaranteed any loans to the service industry before. We were assured that we would be saving 2,000 Canadian jobs. Those 2,000 Canadian jobs did not exist when we got the assurance. There are now no Canadian jobs and the company has gone bankrupt. We appreciate that the Cabinet found it necessary to do this for its own purposes, but the purpose of a board of directors is to manage the affairs of the company, and it is not right to allow Cabinet to override that board if it has made that kind of decision. That is why my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), is attempting to cut back on what the Government wants to do through this Bill.
There are other examples of Crown corporations that are running around without any control whatsoever. I draw to the Chair's attention the Canada Development Investment Corporation which is naturally fathered by a member from the other place who is the only Cabinet Minister from British Columbia.
We on this side note with great amusement that the Canada Development Investment Corporation reports to the House of Commons, the representatives of the people, through the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres). It is amusing because he is not even on the economic committee. At least he was not on that committee when its list of members was last published. One does not know when he would have the opportunity to have these great communications with the Minister from the other place. That is another example of a Crown corporation running around making investments.
There is a man named Joel Bell whom I have always referred to as the pseudo Lee Iacocca of Crown corporations. He will do for Crown corporations what Lee Iacocca did for the Chrysler Corporation. One must understand that there is no bottom line with a Crown corporation. Lee Iacocca had a bottom line and brought the Chrysler Corporation back to health.
We do not have any confidence that the people running the CDIC operation and other Crown corporations will do the kind of jobs that we as Members of Parliament want them to do, basically because they refuse to be accountable. If they were prepared to be accountable to Parliament and if they were not Jack Horners, we would be prepared to go along with some of these things. As long as they refuse the accountability that we as representatives of taxpayers demand, we will continue to fight legislation such as Bill C-l 10.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-l 10, to amend the Export Development Act, as recorded (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 6 and 8 (Mr, Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker. I rise to speak on the two motions proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I enjoyed the address given by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) very much. He put forward a number of observations regarding Crown corporations. The problem of credit, finance and insurance is a very important one in today's financial world. There is a scramble for export markets, and countries from all around the world are working hard to assist their corporations in entering these markets. I see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is in the House, and we know how he tried to inflict a Crown corporation upon us recently, one which would be involved in this very important area.
There is great competition for markets and this presents difficulties. The treasuries of European communities and of the United States are much larger than ours and, as a result, we have to be very aggressive and use some of the methods used by our competitors in export markets.
I wholeheartedly support the amendments proposed by my colleague which deal with accountability to this institution. The Government brings forward legislation for debate in an attempt to get Opposition Parties to agree with it but it asks constantly for more money than it ought to. It takes time to get these measures through the House. The borrowing Bill is

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
an example of that, and now the Government has brought this Bill forward. If the Government and Crown corporations can prove to Members of Parliament that the money is required, the legislation will be passed very quickly. The amount of money being asked for in this legislation brings us to the nub of the question of accountability.
Two Hon. Members who spoke ahead of me mentioned the speech that was referred to in Question Period today. The man who made that speech sat in this House for almost 20 years, but how soon he forgets, Mr. Speaker. I remember many speeches made by Mr. Horner when he spoke about the rights of Members of Parliament and the worth of the institution. Now that he is Chairman of a Crown corporation he seems to feel that that corporation should not allow the Auditor General to look at its books. In committee there have been months of debate on a Bill that will give hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money to that particular corporation. Members of Parliament are not asking to be directly involved in the operation of the railway but they feel that they have a right to know that the money voted in this institution will be properly spent. The Auditor General tells us whether this happens. It is important that Crown corporations be competitive, but we would also like them to be accountable to Parliament.
In this Bill the Government seeks authority to increase the value of loans and loan guarantees issued by Order in Council from $2.5 billion to $10 billion. That is not a small increase. The Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) illustrated for us, in a very picturesque way, what a billion dollars is.
When we look at Orders in Council we see just how irrelevant this institution is becoming. Since January 1 of this year Cabinet has passed 2,789 Orders in Council, all without any reference to Parliament. That authority has been put into legislation over the years and we have passed it. A committee is supposed to examine Orders in Council but considering the volume of them, it is almost impossible for one committee to do this. As a result, Parliament becomes more and more irrelevant. Surely many of these Orders in Council should come to the various committees for examination in detail. When legislation is drafted, surely we should be more concerned about the authority given to the Governor in Council to make certain regulations. It is a very innocent clause in many Bills but it gives unbelievable power to Ministers.
The Government wants to give Cabinet the authority to approve insurance deals that the Export Development Corporation is not prepared to approve. That means that if the board of directors-which the Government has appointed to run the corporation-decrees in its wisdom that a deal ought not to be approved, then Cabinet, in its wisdom, can disagree. There is nothing in the Bill to stop Cabinet from making that decision; it can override the board of directors and approve the deal. It seems to me that a Government ought to find the best people possible to sit on the board of directors and, having done so, it ought to abide by their decision. If the board thinks a deal is a bad one, then I do not see how the Government can say it does not agree. Any interference by the Government must be for political reasons. A bad deal is a bad deal.
I support my colleagues when they say we ought to limit that clause and that if the Government wants to interfere with the board of directors of the corporation, it ought to ask permission of Parliament. The Government spends taxpayers' money for which we are responsible. That accountability is at the centre of this debate, and that is what we are saying. Another thing which disturbs me about the Export Development Corporation is that it seems to be doing some of the work of CIDA. When we look at some of the loans which have been approved in the past few years, we find we have extended financing to INCO, for development of plants in Indonesia and Guatemala, and that is creating jobs which, perhaps, are jeopardized here in this country. We have forest development projects in other countries. If there is a necessity to develop those industries in those countries, that ought to be done under CIDA. The Export Development Corporation should be a lender or a financier of last resort. When the private sector is not able to put this together it should then come to the Export Development Corporation to guarantee its loans, to insure its loans or to refinance those loans. That is what the Economic Council in its report proposed. It is so very important that we have the accountability and control which comes with Parliament.
I would like to conclude by saying that 1 appreciate the speeches of the many Hon. Members of Parliament on this side who are so concerned about this institution and what we make of it in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to express a few words of concern about this Bill which gives the Government more borrowing authority. I have lost confidence in this arrogant and incompetent Government. The reason I say that, Mr. Speaker, is that I happen to be one of those who was not born in this country. 1 came from Poland when I was about five years old, during the Depression. 1 quite appreciate the fact of unemployment and welfare. We have accomplished many things since that Depression. We have brought about social services, pensions and we have put many mechanisms in place so that a depression of the kind we had then will never happen again. But what has this Government done? It has destroyed the lives of two million Canadians who are unemployed today. I know what that feels like. I was one of those who were on welfare when I came from Poland during the Depression. I know what it feels like to go to the grocery store where you cannot even buy a loaf of bread or a quart of milk but you have to make soup out of the same bone two or three times. I have gone through all of that.
It is very hard for me to believe that this Government actually got to be so irresponsible and uncaring for the Canadian people. I can speak with some authority, Mr. Speaker, in that area because I was an elected city alderman in the City of Calgary for ten years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What are your solutions?
September 22, 1983

I am talking about solutions. There are only about five or six Hon. Members on the other side, and you are expressing concern? I am very much referring to the solutions.
I do not interfere with you when you speak. Please have the courtesy to let me, on this side, speak. If you do not like it, you can walk out, because most of your colleagues are out anyway. One more or less will not make any difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You are talking about your own Party, are you not?

If you will listen, you may learn something becaue I was in the labour movement involved with the problems we are faced with today when you were still in diapers. So perhaps you had better listen and maybe you will learn something.
I would like to refer to credibility. I have been an alderman for ten years. I was the chairman of finance and budget in Calgary for two terms. I never pretended I was some sort of an expert in finance, but I was always able to listen, to show some compassion, to cut through some red tape and be able to keep in mind that the people should receive full value for their tax dollars. That is not what is happening in the House of Commons today. The Government has been spending money like drunken sailors. Canadians no longer want to see this Government get more authority to spend money. Canadians want to see this Government get out. They want a new government so they can have hope. As our leader has pointed out many times, we must give back confidence to the business community so it can help rebuild this country and get our factories rolling and Canadians working again.
I have also served as the chairman of operations and development. So 1 say to the Hon. Members opposite, 1 have known accountability and responsibility which we do not have here. 1 have heard expressed many times, and 1 have experienced it myself, this complete loss of confidence in the Liberal Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, say it is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Talk about jobs now.

The Hon. Member opposite is asking about jobs. 1 can say that this Government has put us in this mess. It has been the Government for 15 years, so it certainly cannot blame the Conservatives and it cannot blame world economic conditions. We are living in one of the wealthiest countries in the world. We should not be in the mess we are in today. The problem is that there is no leadership on the other side. There is only one leader and the bureaucrats are running this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Stick to the Bill.
You have nothing to say, my friend, as far as running this Government is concerned, as a backbencher. That is the way it is structured now. That is the way it has become in the last 15 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You have not told us about your solutions.
Export Development Act

I am getting back to accountability, and that is what it is all about. 1 came to be chairman of the land committee. 1 did not pretend to be an expert, but I was able to listen and to reflect the needs of the people of my city at that time. That is what this Government has failed to do. It has failed to reflect the needs of this country.
From there I served on the Calgary Board of Education. 1 served as an elected official as well as a bureaucrat, but accountability existed then very much so, the accountability we do not have here. I am happy that Hon. Members opposite are responding. The reason I have lost respect is that I see there is no justice in this House of Commons. The Ministers are very evasive and incompetent, as far as I am concerned, and that seems to be the name of the game. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is doing a very good job in that area as well. It is a disgraceful situation we have got ourselves into.
1 was elected in the Province of Alberta as a member of the Legislative Assembly, and I have to say that accountability is somewhat lesser in that area, but nothing as compared to what we have in this Government. As a matter of fact, this Government has killed the goose which has laid the golden egg, that is, the oil industry. In fact, it has destroyed the oil industry in this country. It has destroyed the incentive and the backbone of the small business community.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: 1 rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I know we have a rule of relevancy. I do not know if the Hon. Member is looking for a job, but he has been giving us his curriculum vitae. Is that part of the Bill we are discussing?

speechtext: The Chair will pay attention to the Hon. Member's remarks. 1 am sure the Hon. Member has heard the point which has been raised.

Export Development Act

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but get emotional over what is happening in the country and here in the House of Commons. As a matter of fact, they want them out of office, and the sooner the election is called, Mr. Speaker, the better it will be.

If I may, I want to touch a little more on what is really happening right now. You see, you are squirming right now and you are embarrassed about what is realy happening. You cannot stand it.
