Member on the other side for paying attention and being sensitive to what is happening in this country right now. I want to conclude by saying, Mr. Speaker, you are most patient.
More!
Thank you, very much. I enjoyed saying a few words. 1 wanted to say more but I am not going to take advantage of it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on Motions Nos. 6 and 8 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Let me say at the outset, Sir, that the old boy network of the clients of EDC is working well, it is healthy and vibrant. At 7.30 this morning I was talking to a gentleman employed by a large manufacturer who uses the facilities of the EDC for export financing. The company is one of the members of the "club of '62". This chap passed on a message to me that we should pass this Bill, just close our eyes, hold our noses and pass the Bill. That in essence was his message. Maybe he did not say it quite as concisely as I have, but that is what it was all about. He implied that we were sort of holding up some large deal that was going to be financed through the EDC.
I must say he was surprised when 1 advised him that the EDC had adequate financing for the next 18 months, and adequate insurance funding to handle export sales for probably the next 24 months. He was surprised to learn that the Government has the right to guarantee and insure loans up to $3.5 billion and only $460 million has been spent, the Government was asking us to close our eyes, hold our noses and give EDC an additional $10 billion for loan guarantees and insurance. He did not really understand that. He had the impression gained from the management of his company that some large deal they had ready to go out the door, ready to be signed, was being held up until this Bill passed. Well, what a lot of nonsense. It just proves the sort of fraud being perpetrated on the people of Canada.
My friend could not really understand the request for more than three times the present loan and insurance fund. He could not understand it any more than I can. Then I explained to him that we had moved an amendment to cover this matter, in fact to return the loan and insurance guarantee back to $3.5 billion because only $460 million has been used and why should we give the Government $10 billion on top? He could not understand it, and I explained to him our Motion No. 6 and what it was going to do.
I hear my friend across the way and I do not think he has ever had anything to do in the field of commerce with export business, so he should just keep quiet until I am finished. If he wants to come across and ask me about my experience in the export market I will be glad to tell him a few things.
When we began talking about Motion No. 8, Mr. Speaker, I explained that the Government presently has the right to take up to $2.5 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and lend that money to foreign companies, boards, agencies or Government. He was not aware of that, and I went on to explain that even though it had lent only $711 million and it still had $1.8 billion available, in spite of all this the Government was asking us to close our eyes, hold our nose and give it another $10 billion. That is something he could not understand. He was surprised. I said, well, why not go back to your management and ask them what sort of game they are playing here? We believe as strongly as anyone in export business but we do not like being conned, and that is what is happening here. Then I went on to explain to him our Motion No. 8 and
September 22, 1983

why we wanted to keep the limit at $2.5 billion. In essence, we just do not trust the guys across the aisle. That is what it comes down to. That is the bottom line. Give those guys $20 billion to play with and God knows what will happen to it.
The gentleman who called me, Mr. Speaker, and I am not being critical of him because he is a good friend of mine, but he was a messenger. He was a messenger from the boys in the dub who said, "Pass on the line to these guys that you know in the House of Commons that we have to have that export financing right away and that we will go under if we do not get it." I have gone to him and said, "I want you to pass back a message to your friends in the company and tell them that they have more than adequate financing presently in EDC to last them for the next 18 to 24 months regardless of what activity they get involved in."
That is the matter in a nutshell. While I will not say what I have written here because I notice that it is an unparliamentary word and I respect you too much to utter it, Mr. Speaker,
1 just say to those guys to get on with their jobs while we concern ourselves with the accountability to Parliament for this amount of money.
It frightens me when I think of a board of directors, as recommended in this Bill, comprised primarily of bureaucrats who are beholden to the Government for their livelihood and income, having the ability to dip into the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the extent of $20 billion in addition to what they presently have available. That really frightens me because past experience has shown that this is where the Government spending gets out of control. Unless there is a check and balance in Parliament through the Estimates and the budget system, it just disappears.
If the Government would agree to pass the amendments, I am sure my colleagues would agree to expedite the passage of the Bill. However, until we can have some negotiations along that line, I am sure that the fact there are no cheques, no balances, no controls, and no accountability to Parliament and the people of Canada means that we cannot just blindly vote for this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it certainly is a privilege to be able to follow my illustrious colleague, the Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) who is a very successful businessman. 1 am well aware that he has some considerable experience in the export business because of his particular company.
I certainly support Motions Nos. 6 and 8 in the name of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Motion No. 6, which has been well described by the mover, would allow the Government of Canada to increase the limit on promissory notes to $10 billion from the present $3.5 billion. When we look at this motion more closely, we see that the present Government has come to the House of Commons with a request to increase this limit to $10 billion when in fact it has
Export Development Act
not surpassed the present limit. In that case, why does the Government want to increase this limit?
There is no way that we can allow the Government or Crown corporations to continue to grow in the direction which this Government allows. What we have had in Canada from the present Government is a fixation on excessive spending and empire building. This is certainly reflected by the preoccupation of both Ministers and administrators.
Whereas the focus should return to the House of Commons, the opposite has taken place. Crown corporations have become a subgovernment. It seems to me that it is not only improper but immoral for a government to move in the direction of removing from Parliament the means and opportunity of challenging those operations which we feel so strongly are not acting in the best interests of my constituents or the rest of Canada. That is our task as Parliamentarians.
The important issue, as I see it, is accountability to Parliament. This Government, over the years that it has been in power, has given Canadians rising deficits to a projected $31.3 billion this year. The current cost of interest on public debt in 1983 is $700 per capita, or $16,200 per taxpayer. The interest alone on our debt for 1983 will amount to a staggering $17 billion, which 1 believe is one-half limes the amount of the total budget the year 1 entered this hallowed Chamber in the fall of 1972.
How much will it be when Bobby Orr gets here?

We will worry about Bobby Orr, my illustrious friend, later. 1 think you will admit that if he wants to come here, this Chamber is available to all people. All one has to do is to get the nomination and then be elected. I am wondering if my illustrious friend will be here after the next election even though he might get the nomination.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Time will tell.

We will see.
The focus should return to the House of Commons, and 1 want to emphasize that point. The important issue is accountability, and this Government has not been accountable over the years.
With this record of performance, how can we be asked to give another blank cheque as the Government is asking? As many of my colleagues have stated, we are not prepared to give the Government a blanck cheque. We believe it should come before Parliament. If the Government has legitimate reasons and can point out where the expense is required and the money is needed, I believe there would then be a different attitude taken by those of us on this side of the House.
With the increase in the employment of Crown corporations, we must give Parliament more powers of direction, control and scrutiny over Crown corporations to ensure their efficient, effective and accountable performance. When I spoke on this Bill earlier I pointed out that there are well over 300 Crown corporations doing business in Canada. In many cases they are

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
competing with the private sector. If the Crown corporations do not have sufficient funds, the Government is there to bail them out. We know the horror stories of some Crown corporations that are in the red for astronomical amounts.
Why is it that the Government and bureaucratic managers so favour Crown corporations and persist in expanding them and endeavour to form new ones at every opportunity? Why does the Government continue to resort to this corporate form of organization when the private sector time and again is a better instrument? There seems to be a love-hate relationship here. The Government embraces the growth of the Export Development Corporation with wreckless abandonment and seems both incoherent and largely unconcerned about the reasons behind this expansion. But let Hon. Members rest assured that the Progressive Conservative Party is very concerned about the growth of the Export Development Corporation and is attempting to bridal this beast.
Motion No. 8 amends the clause which would allow loans through the Consolidated Revenue Fund to be increased from the present limit of $2.5 billion to $10 billion. It seeks to increase the ceiling for loans and loan guarantees made under Cabinet authority to foreign customers. Again, there is a lack of parliamentary control over these high risk and abnormal transactions.
I maintain, along with many of my colleagues, that accountability must be the cornerstone of the parliamentary system as it is the cornerstone of the fiscal system. The standard of accountability expected of those who deal with the management of moneys and taxes raised is far less weighty and is, in fact, downright sloppy. The annual report of the Auditor General of Canada is full of page after page of horror stories relating instances of this matter. A number of items that were brought out in that report should be recalled now as we debate the merits of this particular Bill and these two amendments.
In Mr. Dye's opinion, over the past six years the actual progress toward better accountability has been limited, particularly as far as Parliament is concerned. In the following quote from the report this is further highlighted:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of government activities has so strained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibilities for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds. The existing legislative framework for creating, monitoring and where necessary, changing the purpose of using the corporate form for achieving public policies objectives can be abused.
We, the Official Opposition, have recognized its abuses and stand for greater scrutiny and control, which is what we are doing about Bill C-l 10 and its implications.
This is what this debate is all about. It is not about whether or not the Progressive Conservative Party is against exporting or foreign trade, it is about the fact that government must be accountable to Parliament. Let me emphasize again that we are very much in favour of foreign trade, helping companies to expand trade and to provide credit where credit is necessary.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating today the amendments to Bill C-110, the Export Development Act, and in particular Motions Nos. 6 and 8. I am pleased to follow my colleague, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) who has been in this House a long time now. He understands the functioning of this House and he has seen it deteriorate over the last number of years. I guess you would be as aware as anybody, Mr. Speaker, that I am one of the Members of this House who is not often on my feet to speak on Bills that I think are not of any consequence. But I am concerned about this Bill. It touches at the very essence of our parliamentary system, and I would like to say a few words about that this afternoon. The way this Bill impinges on our system is a threat to our parliamentary democracy.
Before I go further, I want to make a reference to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who came into the debate earlier this afternoon for about four or five minutes. I could not help but observe that the only people who have spoken this afternoon in this debate are Members of the Official Opposition, the Progressive Conservative Party. We appear to be the only people really concerned about the way this Parliament functions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Filibustering.

Filibuster? Mr. Speaker, we are talking about the essence of parliamentary democracy, a subject which 1 will be getting into in a few moments. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North felt that, because we were challenging the way Crown corporations operate, we were therefore opposed to Crown corporations. He went on to explain how many of them we, as Conservative Governments federally and provincially, have instituted in the past. I think we see the role and feel there is still an effective role for Crown corporations. A Member who has been in the House as long as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North has should understand that we are not opposed to Crown corporations. We are opposed to the way they are being operated under the present Government. That is the problem we see.
From time to time I go into our schools. There are teachers in my constituency in Oxford who are prepared to have me go into the schools because they trust that I will not preach partisan politics to their students. They appreciate that I talk about our system of government. What I talk to them about on the whole is something based on three words: representative parliamentary democracy. I do not doubt for a moment that we are experiencing a type of democracy in Canada now, but it is not the type of democracy that most Canadians want. The kind of democracy practised by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues and the people who control the Liberal Party outside of this House who are not elected shows they are not interested at all in a representative parliamentary democracy. They are interested in a kind of democracy where the powers that be at the centre of that Party are able to control the backbenchers. I could not help noticing that as I sat here this afternoon and watched Members on the
September 22, 1983

Government side. For a while there were as many as two or three, more recently there have been five, eight or ten. I see about six at the present time sitting on the Government side. Two of them are pretty good friends of mine. They are from London. They are two of the triplets from London. The Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) and the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield) were sitting together for quite a long time. They are both very fine gentlemen. But I am disappointed that neither they nor any of their colleagues on the other side have seen fit to get up this afternoon and speak to the very issue that we in the Opposition are talking about. We are not talking about whether the Government needs more money or not. What we are talking about is the accountability of Parliament to what the Government is doing or not doing. That is what we are discussing. Yet, the Liberals do not have the courage to get up and defend what the Government is doing. They are giving tacit approval to what we in the Opposition are saying, namely that they are not accountable to this Parliament. They are unable to defend the fact that they are being accountable to this Parliament. That is a shameful position for people who are representatives of the people of Canada. They are sitting on the Government side and they are not in a position to get up and defend how and to what extent their own Government is being accountable.
The three words, representative parliamentary democracy, are words that have a lot of meaning. I have mentioned already the effect of democracy. Take the words "parliamentary". The essence of that word is that we here in this Chamber make our decisions following talk. Lots of talk goes on here. But we should bear in mind that altogether too often we are prevented from talking in a fashion like this because the Government sees reason to bring in closure and forbids us the opportunity to speak on issues that we feel are of importance to our system here.
Finally, probably the most important word today from the point of view of this debate is the concept of the word "representative". All of us here are representing a certain part of the country. We are here to express the opinions of the people. We are also here to come to decisions and to vote based on what we hear in the debates, Mr. Speaker. It is distressing for me that Members on the Government side, the backbenchers in particular, are not given the opportunity to vote as they see fit. I am sure my friend, the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex, who is sitting today on our side, might well prefer to sit on this side of the House because his philosophies are much in keeping with those of us here. But he is not in a position to say what he would like to say on behalf of the Government because he is not given the choice to represent his own views before the House of Parliament, nor the views of his constituents. 1 think we are just seeing this whole system of ours go down the drain because the people of Canada are beginning to realize and are developing a cynicism which is based on the fact that no longer are we as their representatives reflecting their views.
Export Development Act
I spoke on this Bill just two days ago and mentioned that I spoke to a good friend of some of my colleagues across the way. He was lamenting the fact that the people who are appointed to Crown corporations are no longer representative enough of the private sector. We see in the workings of the various Crown corporations that the Cabinet overrides the decisions of these boards. Yet the Government is asking to have more money. I think that is an intolerable situation. This upsets the private sector and, after all, that is still the prominent part of our economy.
In short, I am here to speak in favour of Motions Nos. 6 and 8 which are attempts on the part of the Opposition to amend this dreadful Bill which will give an opportunity to this Government to spend increasing amounts of money without being accountable to the representatives of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act. I am delighted to follow the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) and the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) who was asked by an Hon. Member across the aisle when Bobby Orr would come to Parliament. That will be decided in the next election.
In particular I would like to speak to Motions Nos. 6 and 8 which are before the House. Motion No. 6 in part reads:
"shall not at any time exceed 3 billion 500 million and I".
Motion No. 8 in part reads:
"shall not at any time exceed 2 billion 500 million and I".
As we are well aware, Bill C-l 10 will give the Government $62 billion of authority. We must rise and continue to speak out on behalf of the people who sent us here, demanding that the Government be accountable. Parliament should not be used for access to $62 billion without a vote on the subject.
In the words of Professor Andre Raynauld of the University of Montreal, the Export Development Corporation is:
-rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire, and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient.
Also, seven years ago the report of the Auditor General noted:
In the majority of Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually nonexistent.
What we are talking about today is accountability: accountability of Government to Parliament, accountability of Members to their constituents, and accountability of Crown corporations to taxpayers.
Approximately four years ago the Lambert report noted:
In examining the bewildering array of Crown agencies we have found that existing provisions for classifying them and for accountability for each category have been rendered obsolete. The resulting state of confusion, if left unattended, will seriously impair the value of these agencies as instruments of public purpose and do further damage to the tenuous and sometimes obscure accountability

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
links that, in varying degrees, they now have with the Government and Parliament.
Last fall the Auditor General noted:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The growing practice of using Crown-owned corporations to conduct a widening range of government activities has so stained the capability of the existing accountability framework that Parliament may not be able to exercise its fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds.
As a Member of Parliament for Malpeque on Prince Edward Island, 1 find that statement hard to accept because as elected representatives we are accountable to our constituents. We have to answer for the stands we take. I believe that the Government should answer to Parliament for the decisions it makes, that Crown corporations should answer to taxpayers and that Members of Parliament have to answer to their constituents.
I operate a business on Prince Edward Island. When 1 go to the bank to borrow money with which to run my business, the bank manager asks me how much I need and for what I need it. Very seldom will he give me more money than 1 need. In fact, 1 need to have good reason before he will even give me the money I want. There is no way that he would give me a line of credit ten times in excess of what I need or a blank cheque to be used for anything I decide in future. It is a good practice. Sometimes when the bank manager gives me a hard time and I have to account to him, I think he is somewhat unreasonable, but upon reflection I realize that because he has made me accountable to him I have managed to stay in business and to be successful. I hope to continue to run a successful business. I have been accountable to someone, someone was there to ensure that I did not go off on a tangent and was unable to pay my bills. The same thing should happen in Parliament. The Government should be accountable to Parliament. Members of Parliament, in their wisdom, should decide how much money the Government will be able to spend or how much it will be able to give to Crown corporations.
I am a relative rookie in the House of Commons, having only been here a little over four years, but I feel quite strongly that the Government does not appreciate the fact that it should be accountable to Parliament. In fact, it should be accountable to the Opposition who voices the concerns of the people of Canada. I cannot emphasize strongly enough how I feel about Bill C-110 and the fact that the Government wants to increase the expenditure limits of the Export Development Corporation. The Government is attempting to circumvent Members of Parliament who were sent here by their constituents to ensure that it did what was best for Canadians.
In the few minutes remaining I would like to stress the fact that the Government has not been doing the job it should be doing. He has done everything he can to undermine the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-l 10, an act to amend the Export Development Act. Bill C-l 10 is a bad Bill. This Bill erodes Parliament's right in the area of accountability and control regarding the public purse, taxpayers' dollars. Through this Bill the Government believes that, as in the old adage of the Divine Right of Kings, tax dollars are its divine right, that the public purse is the property of the Government to do as it pleases with as little reference to Parliament and to outside consultations as it can get away with.
Bill C-l 10 seeks to expand the operational capacity of the Export Development Corporation without need for further reference to Parliament. To add insult to injury, the Government seeks as well to increase the high risk or bad business transactions from $3.5 billion to $10 billion concerning insuring sales, and from $2.5 billion to $10 billion in the case of loans and loan guarantees. To further aggravate the situation, losses incurred under such circumstances are to be paid from the Consolidated Revenue Fund without reference to Parliament.
I can well understand such action being taken in a dictatorial state, but such high-handed action has no place in a democratic country. Unless we stop this continual erosion of democracy by this Government, and soon, democracy will become a dead issue in Canada.
The fact that the Export Development Corporation is not accountable to Parliament is totally unacceptable. It is the taxpayers' money we are talking about and they have the right to know how their money is being spent. To borrow money in
September 22, 1983

the name of Canadian taxpayers and their children without seeking parliamentary authority to do so, cannot be allowed to continue. That is the main principle behind the reason why I refuse to go along with this Bill.
What it really means is that the Government, with this Bill, will have the authority to make any deal it cares to make. The Government will be able to make loans to anyone it wishes without any vote by any Parliament at any time. It also means that the Government may make insurance commitments that are not of a commercial nature to a ceiling of $10 billion. As well, the Government may make loans that are not of a proper commercial nature to a value of almost $10 billion.
There is no question that the Export Development Corporation is, in the words of Professor Andre Raynauld, of the University of Montreal, and I quote:

rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire, and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient.
There is no question that the Export Development Corporation is poorly managed. It is another example of Government having no business in business. For example, in 1982 the 613 employees of EDC had loan transactions with 62 companies and placed slighly in excess of 900 insurance policies. Can anyone name a bank that has 10 employees for every loan customer? For that matter, can anyone name any insurance company in the private sector which issues insurance policies at an annual rate of one and one half policies per employee? Such inefficiency is not possible in the private sector. If it were so, such companies would be out of business in a very short time.
The lack of common sense which EDC is surrounded with would indicate the reasons why it financed lnco developments in Indonesia and Guatemala at the expense of taking precious jobs from Sudbury and Manitoba. A similar foolish financial fiasco had EDC financing forest development projects in Mexico, Poland and Peru in direct competition with Canadian forest products, again taking away jobs from Canadians. Foolishly again, the EDC helped finance the construction of a monument to the Algerian revolution.
One could go on and one about the way EDC conducts its business. The amount of ineptness, inefficiency and lack of common sense present in the management of EDC would be more than enough to send several private enterprises into bankruptcy if it were ever allowed to happen. The amendments to Bill C-110 introduced by our Party would institute some semblance of order and common sense to an already bad Bill.
We advocate that the chairman of EDC be appointed from outside the Public Service and that the number of public servants on the board be restricted to three. However, the Government wants to impose a 15 man board with no limit to the number of public servants on the board and that the chairman be appointed from the Public Service.
Our amendments also cal! for leaving the authorized capital at $1 billion and restricting borrowing to ten times the actual money on hand in the form of paid-in capital and earned surplus. We would also seek to nullify the Government's
Export Development Act
proposed increase regarding the ceiling for loans and loan guarantees made to foreign countries from the present $2.5 billion to $10 billion.
The few minutes that I am allotted to speak do not permit me to go into greater detail regarding the inappropriatness of Bill C-110 and the EDC. Suffice it to say that much has been said and written concerning the Export Development Corporation. Many recommendations have been made for the betterment of EDC. The Economic Council report "Intervention and Efficiency'' devotes a full chapter to the subject of export finance and the EDC.
As well, several reports of the Auditors General over the years have stressed the lack of financial management and control which they term weak and ineffective. The reports found confusion and unaccountability to be the most important problems of EDC and many of the other Crown corporations, which has certainly impaired the value of these agencies as instruments of public service.
All of us in this House are here to represent our constituents in all facets of federal jurisdiction. It is important for us to ensure that our taxpayers are receiving good value for their tax dollars. This must be preserved at all costs if we as Members are to justify our being here in the first place, if we are to do our job diligently and effectively. We will be serving our constituents and our taxpayers as all of us should be serving and carrying on our responsibilities as Members of Parliament by refusing to compromise our responsibility. We can do that by not letting this Bill pass in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, this happens to be a day in my life which I would like to mention because it relates to the Government of the day and the performance of Members of Parliament. Thirty-one years ago today, at about this hour, I was concluding a political campaign to get myself elected, along with my colleagues, to the provincial Legislature of the Province of New Brunswick. It was a successful campaign. I had the pleasure, which 1 have not enjoyed since, of being part of a Government of the Province of New Brunswick which was fiscally responsible and which for the eight years of its term of office reduced the net debt of the Province on an annual basis, that is a claim which this Government certainly cannot make. Nor has it been an objective of this Government that it be fiscally responsible.
This is another Bill which indicates that this Government is not concerned about money. It may well be that it is a hidden instrument to attain some of the objectionable objectives of this Government. I am concerned about the fiscal responsibility of nations and the private banking system when I consider the debt which has been approved by nations which have no hope of paying, whether they be Poland, Argentina, Mexico, Brazil or whatever. There seems to be little likelihood that those accounts will be paid in full in view of the projections of the world economy as they are being made today.

September 22, 1983
Export Development Act
What will be the consequence of the failure by any of these to honour their bills? What will be the consequence of their failure to pay interest down the road? What will be the consequence of their failure to pay capital down the road? What happens? It has been a long while since we have seen a government go bankrupt. In the 1930s, it was necessary for the federal Government to bail Provinces out and assist them to finance. Are we now in this milieu of economic misfortune, about to face again the possibility that governments can go broke? If so, what is the consequence?
I wonder what the policy objective of this Bill is because as yet it has not been mentioned specifically. The policy in general is that we will export more and therefore we will create more jobs, but let us take a look at where these exports might possibly be directed and, what is more, where the credit may be directed.
1 do not think it is improper to ask of the Government, "Is this to be the instrument by which we may, without public approval and without approval of the House, find ourselves extending aid to the North-South program which has been so thoroughly espoused by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the people on that side of the House?" Is this to be the instrument whereby, in spite of the public asking for fiscal responsibility, we may now conceal the spending of public money directly or money borrowed for which the public is directly responsible? Can we be using that money to extend loans to people in the North-South structure of this land?
The maximum amount that is available to the Crown corporation is considered to be $50 billion or perhaps $60 billion, depending on who estimates its needs. Some of this money is to be provided by Government and some of it is to be made available through the opportunity to borrow with the Government guarantees.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if it be the Cabinet decision to make the loan, are we now setting this nation up to give money to, for instance, Cuba? Are we going to give Cuba perhaps $4 billion, $5 billion? It would not be unusual to find ourselves in that position in view of the Prime Minister's approach to, and sympathy for, the communist world. It would not be unusual or impossible for us to assume that under the cover of darkness and behind the secret curtains, the directorate of this corporation might very well choose to lend large sums of money or to extend large sums of export credit to countries such as Cuba under the guise that it is in the best interests of the North-South dialogue and the accomplishment of that policy within this nation alone.
Again, when I reflect on fiscal responsibility, I wonder what this could do to the country. It is this reason among others which makes me ask that the Government come forward and let the accounts of this corporation be examined by elected people. As was pointed out by the last speaker, there is a board over which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has absolutely total control. Basically, the chairman has had control of the meetings of boards of directors of Crown corporations, particularly when the stock was 100 percent owned by the Government as it is in this instance. Now, however, we are going to supplement the chairman's control, and that goes to the point that he can refuse to accept the vote of his committee in its decision-making process.
We now will have a board with a four-to-one ratio of public employees to private members. The responsibility of a public employee is to please his employer. The public employees on this board will not confront the Government with a decision which is not satisfactory to the Cabinet. This is for two reasons; first, because they must please the employer, which is the Government of the day, and second, because they do not want to get fired. They do not want to be contradicted by Cabinet which can overrule them. Therefore, the control is totally in the hands of the Prime Minister.
The likelihood that the Cabinet would have to overrule the board of directors is remote, provided that the board of directors knows the will of Government, and they shall certainly know it. The Government will see to it that they are completely and totally familiar with what is the wish of Government in respect of a particular loan.
This then becomes a bad Bill which does not reflect fiscal responsibility by the Government, nor does it reflect any possibility of the public knowing what goes on. As I have said, my initiation to Government was in a fiscally-responsible provincial Government. At the present time I find myself in an environment in which fiscal responsibility is just not considered desirable in respect of the accomplishment of the political objectives of a crew of elected members who think they have a halo over their heads and a right to govern and to hell with the public and its better interests.
1 want to know, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to use this Bill as a negotiating instrument at all. When we do extend credit to help Governments and nations and peoples of those nations, are we going to use this to try to overcome some of the unfavourable trade situations in which we find ourselves? I think 1 must return again to the agricultural picture. I recall an instance when 1 happened to be asked to go into the storage room of the dining room of this House of Commons. Among other things which I saw there were canned fruit salads from two nations. One of those products arrived from overseas at a cost less than our cost of packaging and processing the product. That would leave nothing for the producer of some of the fruits which could have been incorporated in that mixture.
If we are to go into the world of trade with $50 billion, do we have the pledge of the Government that we will try to negotiate a better position for our agricultural producers? The agricultural producers of the land find themselves now marketing in Canadian markets which are open to virtually the world at prices which are not relative to our cost of production. Are we then going to try to negotiate some trade opportunities which will be supported by our export credit extensions? Will the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) participate in this and help our farming community?
What is the purpose of this Bill? Is it for North-South relations and a blind way to spend money with nobody knowing? Is it the instrument by which we will get better trade
September 22, 1983

deals with other countries of the world to help the farmers, the fishermen, the manufacturers and the foresters? Why the secrecy? Why does the Government not come forward, Mr. Speaker? The people of the nation need to know these things if they are to spend this many billions of dollars under a blanket where nobody can see it.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-SOVIET AIRCRAFT INTRUSIONS. (B) MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL CIVIL AVIATION ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the heinous attack by a Soviet jet fighter on a Korean Airlines 747 with the loss of 269 lives, 1 asked the Government on September 15 whether it intended to initiate measures at the International Civil Aviation Organization to establish new international agreements on procedures regarding sovereign airspace intrusions, including mandatory visual identification and central command control, before action by a sovereign nation, in order to prevent further tragic loss of life and further destabilization of an already tense international climate.
1 am pleased that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais), in his first response in his new portfolio, demonstrated enough integrity to bring my representation to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) as he promised. I am also extremely pleased to see that the Minister of Transport took my suggestion and on September 20 proposed that ICAO draft a convention expanding and strengthening the international rules of interception. I commend the Minister on recognizing such an important initiative in this crucial matter of rules governing sovereign airspace. A new international convention needs to be established to strictly govern the interception of civilian aircraft and prevent hostile acts by military aircraft. The convention must have teeth to ensure respect for and compliance with its procedures.
September 22, 1983

This entire issue has a broader scope to it, that of east-west relations and the nature of the Soviet Union. The only surprise in the destruction of the Korean Boeing 747 and the taking of 269 innocent civilian lives, should be that the Soviets grossly miscalculated international public and governmental response to the incident. This incident, and the decisions taken, are indicative that the Soviet decision-making process may be becoming increasingly under the influence of the Soviet military establishment. For at least the past three decades the elite of Soviet youth have been channelled into the military. While the older intellectual and power-broker mandarins still remain in ultimate control, Andropov has yet to consolidate the traditional authority vested in his office.
The next generation of leadership of the power-brokers in the Soviet Union may be emerging from within the new and younger military establishment. Therefore, in dealing with the Soviet Union it must be recognized that: first, the Soviet Union has an inherent paranoia and a collective inferiority complex regarding its own security as a result of a history of having its territory overrun and overwhelmed by foreign powers; second, the newly emerging Soviet establishment through internal education and experience, has had limited access to and limited understanding of western values; and third, this new establishment has its own set of values based on a tight, closed, technocratic and totalitarian view of itself and of the individual's relationship and role within the state.
Negotiating from the rule of law and good faith alone is not sufficient in order to deal with barbaric power-brokers whose uncivilized values allow the unleashing of unrepentant forces of destruction against innocent unarmed commercial civil aviation in a supposed time of peace. We must not allow this massacre to pass without the reparations of concrete and meaningful international agreements to further stabilize and assure the peace of the international community. It is with this perspective and approach to the issue one must also look to guarding the sovereign integrity of both Canadian and NORAD airspace.
The Minister of National Defence in response to my question regarding the 77 Soviet incursions into NORAD airspace so far this year, indicated that the premise of my question was not accurate in that "there has not been any entry within Canadian airspace by any Russian aircraft" but that there had been incursions into the Canadian Air Defence Identification Zone. 1 am fully aware of this. NORAD airspace of course includes the CADIZ as well as the Great Britain-lceland-Greenland gap and the Defence Early Warning Identification Zone (DEWIZ) in our northern Territories. The DEW1Z has not yet been violated by Soviet aircraft; that we know of. I appreciate that the Minister is new to his post, and 1 am grateful that he took time to be briefed on this important issue. His response, however, revealed that he possesses the facts without the benefit of comprehension of the subtlety the question involved and which regrettably caused him to misrepresent and distort the premise of my inquiry.
Adjournment Debate
The comprehensive facts remain that Canada is less able to secure national sovereignty at the present time than ever before, and that given the increasing militarization and aggressiveness of the Soviet Union, the Government should honour its commitments to NATO by entering into a bilateral program with the United States to update the efficacy of the northern warning program, as well as bringing our defence spending up to speed, above the level of countries other than Luxemburg, by meeting our 3 per cent GNP commitment to NATO. For the Soviet Union, being a superpower means never showing weakness. The need not to display weakness explains why the Soviets shot the plane down in the first place.
The Soviet Union has perpetuated "the superpower myth", that the two superpowers are equal and therefore equally malevolent. Many people in democratic nations are seduced by this double standard and the continual KGB disinformation campaigns. By accusing KAL Flight 007 of spying, the Soviets are engaging in a game of beggaring the question. The point here is that 269 civilian lives were systematically liquidated by a political system which puts a different value on human life than we in western democracies do. We must understand that different value system and undertake measures to secure our value system from the excesses of another.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-SOVIET AIRCRAFT INTRUSIONS. (B) MEETING OF INTERNATIONAL CIVIL AVIATION ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish personally, to congratulate the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) on his appointment as co-defence critic. 1 look forward to hearing constructive questions from him in the future knowing his interest in subjects of a military nature.
1 believe the Minister, in his response on September 15, answered the Hon. Member's questions thoroughly. However, it is worth repeating some of the points the Minister made, especially concerning the nature of Soviet military aircraft activity off Canada's east coast. Soviet military aircraft, primarily long-range Maritime patrol aircraft, en route between the Soviet Union and Cuba, occasionally intrude into Canada's Air Defence identification Zone known as CADIZ off the east coast. The zone is international, not sovereign Canadian airspace, which is defined as that area 19.3 kilometres from the shoreline.
Canadian Forces interceptors are scrambled to identify, observe and escort intruding Soviet military aircraft out of the zone. However, it is worth underlining that there have been no intrusions of Soviet military aircraft in Canadian sovereign airspace. The photographs the Hon. Member has seen in the press were taken on such missions.
With regard to the U.S. Government's intention to upgrade the DEW Line, this information has been common knowledge for some time. Indeed, discussions between Canada and the U.S. on the modernization of the NORAD system have been going on for some time and formal negotiations are now underway between the Department of National Defence and the U.S. Department of Defence, with a view to determining how best to upgrade all component systems, not just the DEW Line, making up the air defence capability of both countries on this continent.

September 22, 1983
Adjournment Debate
In closing, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the rules of engagement for the interception by military aircraft are in the public domain and that special rules and regulations governing interceptions under NORAD are, for the most part, classified but follow a commonsense, careful and cautious approach.
The Hon. Member is aware that Canada is taking a leading role at the International Civil Aviation Organization meeting in Montreal and has proposed that practical measures be adopted which would govern the interception of civilian planes and prohibit criminal acts by military aircraft. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) has consulted with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) on these issues because of the obvious interest of this Department.
The assembly of the International Civil Aviation Organization is currently considering the recommendations made by the Canadian delegation to this assembly.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FINANCE-INDEXED SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON TAX CHANGES
FINANCE-INDEXED SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON TAX CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 19 last, I had occasion to ask a question of the Minister of State for Finance with respect to the introduction of the Indexed Security Investment Plan.
It was announced in the budget of April 19, that that plan would commence on October 1 next. Indeed on September 7, the Minister stated in a press release that although the ISIP Program would not commence until October 1, 1983, it is important to notify prospective administrators and participants of these changes in the April draft legislation that may be of interest to them. He also stated that he intends to make a further revised draft of legislation public as soon as possible.
I had asked the question because this indexed Investment Security Plan is one of the Most dramatic changes to our Income Tax Act since the tax reform of 1971. In effect, the concept of this plan is that those who invest in stocks traded on the stock market, publicly traded shares, will be able to put those shares in a plan that will index the capital gains and index the losses. Taxes will be paid on the indexed gain. In other words, after inflation is taken into account they will pay taxes on the gain but only the real gain, not the inflationary gain. The real gain may be very small. They will pay half rate taxes on the real gain.
Under this system they are also entitled to deduct their real losses. The losses can be deducted from any income source, not just at the rate of $2,000 a year. The effect is that of those who trade in publicly traded shares and use the Indexed Security Investment Plan, the rich, capable, wealthy, the big traders and those who have lots of money will not pay capital gains tax the way we pay capital gains tax. We will have to pay tax on inflationary gains but these people will be privileged.
The system will be introduced on October 1 without this House of Commons ever seeing the legislation. The Minister of Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) announced details of the information that administrators of the ISIP Plan will be required to report to Revenue Canada. While reporting forms are yet to be finalized, it is expected they will be similar to existing T4 and T5 reporting forms. In other words, this procedure is in motion and ready to go. The administrators of the plan and the big brokerage houses such as Pitfield MacKay and Wood Gundy will know about it but the House of Commons will not know about it. We will not be told what the legislation is all about. It is in Justice right now. Mr. Redden in the Minister's department cannot give us the material. After all we are only Members of Parliament. This is a massive income tax change and what does the Minister of State say? "I would add, however, it is our intention to bring forward the legislation as rapidly as possible." Well, isn't that nice. This is one of the most dramatic changes in the Income Tax Act, a change that is not necessarily unanimously accepted in the investment community. I would point out that Lyman Maclnnis, a senior partner of Touche Ross & Partners calls the ISIP:
-a hell of a lot of bureaucratic machinery giving the benefit to investors who least need help.
Let me emphasize that; it is giving the benefit to investors who least need help. Patricia Johnston of the organization for small business has said that if we are going to do this for the big fat cats, we had better do something for individual owners of shares in privately held companies. We better do something for landowners, farmers and fishermen too.
The system is going ahead. It will be in place on October 1 as far as the investment community is concerned. The forms will be out to them, possibly or possibly not. The regulations will be in their hands, possibly or possibly not. But for sure they will not be in our hands. This House of Commons will not have dealt with the matter. Indeed, the Bill will not even have been introduced.
What we have been calling for is parliamentary control over the taxing system and the borrowing system. We cannot as Members on this side accept this attitude from this Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-INDEXED SECURITY INVESTMENT PLAN. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON TAX CHANGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Indexed Security Investment Plan and the process which the Liberal Government has followed in relation to it is a model for good development of important tax changes. Let me say right at the beginning, if the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is not informed about this plan then he should be ashamed to cash his pay cheque. He claims to be a finance critic yet somehow he has not been able to read a Green Paper that was issued 18 months ago, or listen to the recommendations of the Lortie Commission which came in a year ago, or read the recommendations that were contained in the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) last April, or read the proposals in a detailed Ways and Means Motion filed last
September 22, 1983

April, or read a September 7 press release which came out while he was away galavanting on his holidays, or indeed, listen to the feedback that comes from investors who are very supportive.
This legislation has been suggested, debated and virtually written by the very taxpayers and investment community it should serve. New ideas are, of course, going to come forward in the next few days in the form of draft legislation. October 1 is the Government target date for that. These new ideas as announced in the September 7 press release will contain some technical changes.
These changes are a result of consultation. In this case consultation with the Toronto Stock Exchange Options Committee, a group I think we want to listen to, even if the Hon. Member does not think we should be talking to them. I believe a new open consultative budget process has been put into play over the last two years. We saw it prior to the April budget when the Minister of Finance spoke to every possible interest group he could find. The applause for that budget reflected the widespread consultation that he carried out. We saw it with the federal sales tax proposal, with the charities proposals and with a myriad of other proposals of the Government. The Indexed Security Investment Plan is a result of open government. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South should look for ways to take part in that positive process.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT ANNUAL REPORT OF DEPARTMENT BE TABLED. (B) ORGANIZATIONS' APPEARANCES BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 16, I directed a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) asking when he was planning to table the annual report of the Department, or any other report dealing with the Department of Veterans Affairs in order that we could obtain an order of reference to enable the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs to meet. To date nothing has been tabled, and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs is still not able to meet.
Many recommendations and suggestions by various veterans' organizations should be discussed with a view to implementing such legislation. Veterans are still encountering many difficulties. The more years that pass without any solutions to these problems, the more serious their situation will become. Not meeting to discuss what can be done to assist veterans only makes it appear that the Government is not concerned with their hardships. Perhaps the Minister should glance at the "Last Post" in the Legion magazine. He will see that we lose more of our veterans every day, and the majority of these people and their families have not received what they should in recognition of what they have done for our country.
I have letters from veterans organizations requesting the opportunity to appear before the Committee. The National Council of Veterans Associations in Canada indicated a wish to submit a brief dealing with the basic rate of pension, the aging veterans program, and the continuation of pensions to
Adjournment Debate
widows at the married rate for one year following the death of the pensioners.
The Council would also like to furnish the views of the 13 member associations to the Committee regarding the Department of Veterans Affairs and its agencies. We in the Progressive Conservative Party feel there are many shortfalls in the present legislation, and we feel there is a definite need for the Committee to meet so that we may develop answers to overcome the shortfalls.
The Royal Canadian Legion also made recommendations which should be looked into. It has made suggestions regarding the aging veterans program, war veterans allowance interest exemption, Canadian war veterans living outside of Canada and others. If the Minister took time to consider them, I am sure he would agree that these ideas would if implemented be of significant value to veterans.
I am sure, the Minister is aware that because of constantly changing conditions legislation that works for today may not be suitable for tomorrow. I believe we should be able to make amendments to legislation quickly and easily so that those veterans being affected will not be forced to suffer. For this reason we should always have available an order of reference enabling us to meet when necessary to discuss what we can do to assist our veterans.
I further believe that now is a necessary time to meet particularly when there are so many issues which need to be addressed by the Committee and, most important, since the Committee Chairman was contacted directly asking that the opportunity be given to organizations such as the National Council of Veterans Association to appear. With the Royal Canadian Legion, the National Council of Veterans Association and 13 member associations ready to appear before the Committee with recommendations which would be beneficial to the welfare of veterans, surely the Minister will waste no more time in tabling the report immediately so that veterans can begin enjoying what they have earned.
On June 6, 1983 I informed the House that my Conservative colleagues and I feel that veterans deserve better treatment and that a step toward their receiving better treatment would be to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act as quickly as possible. We therefore requested that the Act be revised on the return of the House in September, providing ample time for the Minister and his Department to draft the necessary changes to the legislation. The reply received was that the review was making good progress and the Minister anticipated that legislative proposals would be ready for consideration either in the fall or next spring.
Needless to say, we and thousands of veterans are still waiting. It seems that veterans are always made to wait. They are forced to wait for improvements to legislation, just as they are forced to wait for their pensions. I realize the Minister has stated the delay in processing pension applications has been significantly reduced. However, if my Private Member's Bill, Bill C-641, an Act to amend the Pension Act, was adopted by the House veterans would have one less thing to wait for.

September 22, 1983
Adjournment Debate
My Bill would impose a 90 day limit at the initial stage and a 45 day limit at each of the two levels in the appeal process. If a decision was not made within any of those periods, the applicant would be automatically awarded the full amount claimed by him. We are certainly not at a loss for veterans issues to be discussed in committee. 1 therefore recommend that the Minister table the report so that we can get right down to business and begin improving the conditions for veterans.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roland de Corneille (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST THAT ANNUAL REPORT OF DEPARTMENT BE TABLED. (B) ORGANIZATIONS' APPEARANCES BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to this question directed to us in the adjournment debate; a question that was directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) on June 16, 1983, concerning the annual report of the Department, 1 wish to advise the House that the report will be ready for tabling between the end of October and the middle of November.
In addition to the comments of the Minister at the time on the issue of Indian veterans, I wish to add that the Minister has met with both the Alberta Indian Veterans Association and Saskatchewan Indian Veterans Association and he has heard their concerns. 1 would like to state also that following consultations between native representatives and departmental officials, Indian veterans have been invited to bring individual complaints to the attention of the Department of Veterans
Affairs. That is the subject of the question that was posed. A mechanism has been established to investigate and respond to every complaint so presented. Also, the Department has identified counsellor positions where the basic requirements would include a good knowledge of the native culture. Five such positions are now staffed by counsellors with a native background.
While the Minister has offered his support to the Indian veteran organizations, he has had to tell them that Veterans Affairs has no authority to make funds available to support their activities. They have been referred to other Government agencies which provide funding to certain organizations.
In closing, I would like to reiterate the Minister's rejection of the Hon. Member's assertion of a breakdown in communications between the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs and the various veterans organizations regarding their appearance before the committee. As the Hon. Member knows, or should know, it has always been the practice of the Chairman and Members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs to meet with any organizations that wishes to appear before the Committee.
